The information on this page is aimed at people who are experiencing antisocial behaviour. You can also read guidance for professionals working to address antisocial behaviour.
...
Antisocial behaviour includes criminal and non-criminal behaviour. This could be:
...
- threatening, harassing or unruly behaviour such as drunkenness and loitering in public spaces
- drug use – and the mess and disruption that can go with it
- vandalism, graffiti, fly-tipping and littering
- disruptive neighbours consistently playing loud music or letting their dog bark all night
...
## Report antisocial behaviour
...
There are different ways to report antisocial behaviour.
...
Call 101 to report a non-emergency incident to the police. You can also report antisocial behaviour on the Police.UK website.
...
Check your local council’s website to find out what types of antisocial behaviour you can report. This could include:
...
- vandalism

- rowdy neighbours
- abandoned cars
- persistent dog barking
- alcohol related nuisance
...

...

...

## Request an anti-social behaviour case review
...

...

...
- share information about the case
- review what action has been taken
- decide whether there are more actions that can be taken
...

...

...

...

...
If you report antisocial behaviour, you can expect an agreed level of service as described in the anti-social behaviour principles. The principles set out a consistent approach to dealing with antisocial behaviour in local communities.
pages.summary:
Summary tailored to your query:
- The GOV.UK guidance on antisocial behaviour covers support for victims, including harassment and disruptive conduct, even when it’s non-criminal.
- Harassment and slander from a family member (in your case, a teenage sister) can fall under antisocial behaviour. The page explains how to report and what actions agencies can take.
- Reporting options:
  - Call 101 for police non-emergency incidents or use the Police.UK website.
  - Check your local council’s site for types of reportable antisocial behaviour (e.g., vandalism, noisy neighbours, persistent dog barking, alcohol-related nuisance) and how to report them.
  - If issues occur in a building, report to your council or housing association.
  - If a crime is involved, you can report anonymously to Crimestoppers.
- If behaviour is persistent, you can request an anti-social behaviour case review (formerly “community trigger”) to have agencies review the case and consider further actions.
- Get support and advice from organisations listed on the page for antisocial behaviour guidance in England and Wales.
- The guidance promotes a consistent service standard (anti-social behaviour principles) for the approach to cases.

Practical next steps for your situation:
1) Document incidents: dates, times, what was said or done, witnesses, any evidence (texts, messages, recordings where legal).
2) Report to the police non-emergency line (101) or online if harassment is continuing. If you’re uncomfortable, start with your local council or housing association if the issue involves shared housing.
3) Consider requesting an anti-social behaviour case review via your local police force or council if harassment is persistent and not resolving.
4) Seek practical support:
   - Legal advice on harassment and safeguarding for your mum.
   - Citizens Advice or local charities offering domestic/teen-related harassment support.
5) If slander constitutes a crime (defamatory statements that cause harm) or threats, consider documenting and, if appropriate, seeking legal advice about defamation or protective measures.

Note: This answer focuses on the UK guidance for antisocial behaviour and reporting channels. If you’re outside England/Wales or need more urgent, personalized help, specify your location and we can tailor steps further.

Summary:
The Citizens Advice page explains your right to respect for private and family life under Article 8 of the Human Rights Act 1998. It covers how the right protects your private life, home, and correspondence, including privacy at home and at work (e.g., phone tapping, email/internet monitoring, CCTV). CCTV use by neighbours can implicate Article 8, and the right is qualified, meaning public authorities (and others with public duties) can interfere with it if necessary to protect the wider public interest or others’ rights. pages.summary:
Summary:
The page explains housing harassment under UK law, including when behavior by a landlord or others creates an intimidating, hostile, degrading, humiliating, or offensive environment or violates your dignity. Harassment can be based on conduct you didn’t want or that has the effect (purpose or effect) of making you feel unlawful or disrespected, regardless of the mover’s intent. It covers discrimination (including by landlords) and unwanted sexual conduct, and notes that harassment does not have to relate to a protected characteristic. Examples include persistent intrusions, intimidating visits, or unwanted behavior in or around your home; even actions by someone like a subtenant or a landlord can be actionable. If you’re facing harassment, you may contact your local council housing department or the police, especially if the behavior includes criminal harassment such as interfering with services or repeated nighttime visits. The guidance emphasizes documenting incidents and seeking appropriate remedies or protection under the Equality Act 2010.

What this means for your situation:
- If a building management director’s adult daughter walks her dog daily along a narrow pathway directly outside your ground-floor windows, and this feels intrusive or intimidating, it could constitute harassment under the Equality Act if the behavior creates an offensive or intimidating environment or violates your dignity.
- Consider gathering evidence of the incidents (dates, times, description, impact).
- You can potentially address this by requesting written communication with the manager, seeking a change in access/paths, or escalating to the housing department or police if the behavior amounts to criminal harassment (e.g., persistent disruption, intimidation, or interference with services).
- Harassment does not need to be related to a protected characteristic to be actionable.

Summary:

- The referenced section (Police directions stopping harassment near a resident’s home) authorizes a constable to issue directions to people outside or near a dwelling to prevent harassment or distress to a resident.
- A direction can require someone to leave the vicinity of the premises or not return for up to 3 months, with possible conditions and exceptions.
- The direction may be given orally and can apply to multiple people; violation can lead to criminal penalties (up to 3 months’ imprisonment or a fine, or both).
- This provision is about police powers to curb harassment or intimidation that occurs in or around a resident’s home, not about civil nuisance or privacy rights in general.

Relevance to your scenario (privacy and intimidation inside home):
- The law targets harassment/ distress around a dwelling, which can include actions near a resident’s home that are meant to intimidate or harass.
- It provides a potential remedy if someone’s presence by a dwelling is causing harassment or alarm, allowing the police to direct those individuals to leave the vicinity.

Notes:
- For non-criminal privacy concerns (e.g., persistent proximity, nuisance behavior) you may also consider civil options or local authority nuisance/anti-social behaviour provisions.
- If you’re dealing with ongoing intrusion or intimidation, you can contact local police and request a harassment/alarm assessment under this framework; you may need to demonstrate reasonable grounds to believe harassment or distress is occurring.

# Legal aid

Skip contents

# Domestic abuse

You might be able to get legal aid if you have evidence that you or your children have experienced domestic abuse and you cannot afford to pay legal costs.

## What counts as domestic abuse for legal aid

Domestic abuse includes:

- controlling behaviour
- emotional abuse
- financial control, for example being stopped from accessing a joint bank account
- someone harassing, threatening or hurting you or your child

The abuse could be from a partner, ex-partner, or family member.

If you’re not sure, you can check how to recognise domestic abuse.

## Providing evidence

You’ll usually need to provide evidence to show that you or your children have experienced domestic abuse.

You can ask for evidence from:

- the courts
- the police
- a multi-agency risk assessment conference (MARAC)
- social services
- a health professional, for example a doctor, nurse, midwife, psychologist or health visitor
- a refuge manager
- a domestic abuse support service
- your bank, for example credit card accounts, loan documents and statements

highlights:
Driving disqualifications: Overview - GOV.UK

Skip to main content

# Driving disqualifications

Skip contents

# Overview

You can be banned (disqualified) from driving if you are either:

- convicted of a driving offence
- get 12 or more penalty points (endorsements) within 3 years

You’ll get a summons in the post that tells you when you must go to court.

Some disqualification rules are different in Northern Ireland.

This guide is also available in Welsh (Cymraeg).

## How long a driving ban will last

The court will decide how long the disqualification will last, based on how serious they think the offence is.

You can be banned from driving if you already have 12 or more penalty points on your licence. Your ban can last:

- 6 months, if you get 12 or more penalty points within 3 years
- 12 months, if you get a second disqualification within 3 years
- 2 years, if you get a third disqualification within 3 years

## Disqualified for 56 days or more

If you’re disqualified for 56 days or more you must apply for a new licence before driving again.

You might also have to retake your driving test or take an extended driving test before getting your full licence. The court will tell you if you have to do this.

## Disqualified for less than 56 days

View your driving licence record online to check the disqualification. You cannot drive until it has ended.

You do not need to apply for a new licence before you can drive again.

## Disqualification outside Great Britain

You cannot drive in Northern Ireland and the Isle of Man if you’ve been banned from driving on your Great Britain driving licence.

This is called ‘mutual recognition of disqualification’. Disqualified drivers from Northern Ireland and the Isle of Man are also banned from driving in Great Britain.

# Penalty points (endorsements)

Skip contents

# Overview

The courts can fine you and ‘endorse’ your driving record with penalty points if you’re convicted of a motoring offence.

This guide is also available in Welsh (Cymraeg).

The endorsement and penalty points are put on your driver record. View your driving licence record to see what penalty points you have and when they’ll be removed.

Endorsements must stay on your driving record for 4 or 11 years, depending on the offence.

You can be disqualified from driving if you build up 12 or more penalty points within a period of 3 years. There are different rules for new drivers.

A non-endorsable offence is a motoring offence where you’re disqualified from driving, but you do not get any penalty points.

If you get no penalty points but are disqualified from driving for 56 or more days, you will have to pay to renew your licence. You can only renew your licence after the disqualification period ends.

Endorsement codes and processes in Northern Ireland are different.

Summary:

- This section of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 (Section 28 on Delivery of Goods) sets default terms for any sales contract.
- Unless the trader and consumer agree otherwise, the contract includes a term that the trader must deliver the goods.
- Delivery must be:
  - without undue delay, and
  - no later than 30 days after the contract is entered into, unless another time is agreed.
- If the trader fails to deliver as agreed, the consumer may have remedies:
  - If delivery is essential or the consumer told the trader delivery was essential before the contract, the consumer may treat the contract as at an end (i.e., cancel) and the trader must refund all payments without undue delay.
  - In other circumstances, the consumer may specify a reasonable period for delivery and require delivery within that period. If delivery still fails, the consumer may treat the contract as at an end and get refunds for goods not delivered or for rejected/cancelled items.
- If the contract is ended under these provisions, the trader must reimburse all payments without undue delay. If the consumer does not end the contract but still cancels/rejects goods, refunds apply to the cancelled/rejected items.

Practical takeaways for your scenario (England):
- If a dealership has not provided a delivery date or finance documents, you likely have default delivery rights under the Act. The trader should deliver within 30 days unless you agreed a different time.
- If delivery is not provided and delivery was essential (or you made that clear before contracting), you may be entitled to treat the contract as ended and receive a full refund.
- If delivery is not brought within a reasonable period you set (or within 30 days if none was agreed), you may have grounds to end the contract and get refunds for all payments.
- If you do not end the contract, you can still cancel or reject goods and obtain refunds for those items.

What to do next:
- Document dates: order date, agreed delivery date (if any), any communications about delivery or finance documents.
- Send a written notice to the dealer requesting delivery by a specific date or, if they cannot comply, stating that you consider the contract at an end and request a full refund (as per the Act).
- If there is no remedy, contact Citizens Advice or GOV.UK consumer guidance for formal steps and consider small claims/cdispute resolution if refunds are not provided.

Note: The above reflects rights under the Consumer Rights Act 2015, especially section 28 on delivery of goods. If the issue concerns finance documents or a failed funding arrangement, you may also need to consider other consumer protections or contract law aspects. For precise advice, consult Citizens Advice or a solicitor.

- The Consumer Contracts Regulations (UK 2013) require traders to deliver goods without undue delay and, unless a delivery date is agreed, within 30 days of the contract.

# If you’re in an accident

If you have an accident causing damage or injury you must give the following to anyone with ‘reasonable grounds for requiring them’, for example an insurance company:

- your name and address
- the vehicle registration number

You also need to give the owner’s name and address if the vehicle is not yours.

You must report the accident to the police within 24 hours if you do not give your details at the time of the accident.

You must also report the accident to your insurance company, even if you’re not planning to make a claim.

## Accidents with uninsured motorists

You should tell the police if you have an accident with someone who’s not insured.

Your insurance company will also be able to give you more advice.

In your case:

- Inform the owner politely to ensure your contact details are complete (name, address, registration) if not already provided.

# Change a will after a death

You can change a person’s will after their death, as long as any beneficiaries left worse off by the changes agree.

If there’s no will the law decides who inherits. You can make changes to the inheritance in the same way as if there’s a will.

Any changes to the will must be completed within 2 years of the death.

You can change a will to:

- reduce the amount of Inheritance or Capital Gains Tax payable
- provide for someone who was left out of the will
- move the deceased’s assets into a trust
- clear up any uncertainty over the will

## What you need to do

To change a will you’ll need to make a ‘variation’.

You do not need a formal document or deed - you can write a letter as long as it meets these conditions.

If the variation means there’s more Inheritance Tax to pay, you must send a copy to HM Revenue and Customs(HMRC) within 6 months of making it.

You do not need to send a copy to HMRC if the variation does not change the amount of Inheritance Tax due.

highlights:
Workplace bullying and harassment - GOV.UK

Skip to main content

# Workplace bullying and harassment

Bullying and harassment is behaviour that makes someone feel intimidated or offended. Harassment is unlawful under the Equality Act 2010.

Examples of bullying or harassing behaviour include:

- spreading malicious rumours
- unfair treatment
- picking on or regularly undermining someone
- denying someone’s training or promotion opportunities

Bullying and harassment can happen:

- face-to-face
- by letter
- by email
- by phone

## The law

Bullying itself is not against the law, but harassment is. This is when the unwanted behaviour is related to one of the following:

- age
- sex
- disability
- gender reassignment
- marriage and civil partnership
- pregnancy and maternity
- race
- religion or belief
- sexual orientation

## What employees should do if they’re bullied or harassed

Employees should see if they can sort out the problem informally first. If they cannot, they should talk to their:

- manager
- human resources (HR) department
- trade union representative

If this does not work, they can make a formal complaint using their employer’s grievance procedure. If this does not work and they’re still being harassed, they can take legal action at an employment tribunal.

They could also call the Acas (Advisory, Conciliation and Arbitration Service) helpline for advice:

Acas helpline Telephone: 0300 123 1100 Textphone: 18001 0300 123 1100 Monday to Friday, 8am to 6pm Find out about call charges

You can also read Acas guidance on discrimination and bullying.

## Employers’ responsibilities

Employers are responsible for preventing bullying and harassment - they’re liable for any harassment suffered by their employees.

Anti-bullying and harassment policies can help prevent problems. Acas has produced guidance for employers on preventing and handling bullying and harassment.

Summary:

The Citizens Advice page explains what constitutes harassment and bullying at work and how the law (Equality Act 2010) applies. Key points:

- Harassment is unwanted conduct that creates an intimidating, hostile, degrading, humiliating, or offensive environment, or violates your dignity.
- Bullying can amount to harassment, especially if tied to a protected characteristic (e.g., race/ethnicity). You can take action under the Equality Act if the conduct relates to a protected characteristic (like race or nationality) or is otherwise harassment.
- The conduct can be directed at you or create a hostile environment even if you’re not the target of the characteristic itself (e.g., a racist poster affecting you).
- Purpose or effect and reasonableness matter: you need to show the conduct had the purpose or effect of violating dignity or creating an offensive environment, and that it was unwelcome.
- If harassment is by a colleague, both the harasser and the employer can be legally responsible (vicarious liability) under the Equality Act.
- There may also be overlaps with hate crime/hate incidents; guidance is available for those cases too.

If you’re in a construction-site context with a supervisor who is racist and abusive daily, this guidance indicates you may have grounds to pursue legal action under the Equality Act for harassment, and your employer could be liable for the supervisor’s conduct. For tailored steps, consider reporting the incident internally, seeking formal harassment/bullying procedures, and contacting Citizens Advice or legal services for specific advice and remedies in the UK.

Skip to main content

# Discrimination: your rights

Skip contents

# Discrimination at work

The law protects you against discrimination at work, including:

- dismissal
- employment terms and conditions
- pay and benefits
- promotion and transfer opportunities
- training
- recruitment
- redundancy

Some forms of discrimination are only allowed if they’re needed for the way the organisation works, for example:

- a Roman Catholic school restricting applications for admission of pupils to Catholics only
- employing only women in a health centre for Muslim women

## Disability

If you’re disabled you have the same rights as other workers. Employers should also make ‘reasonable adjustments’ to help disabled employees and job applicants with:

- application forms, for example providing forms in Braille or audio formats
- aptitude tests, for example giving extra time to complete the tests
- dismissal or redundancy
- discipline and grievances
- interview arrangements, such as providing wheelchair access, communicator support
- making sure the workplace has the right facilities and equipment for disabled workers or someone offered a job
- promotion, transfer and training opportunities
- terms of employment, including pay
- work-related benefits like access to recreation or refreshment facilities

## What you can do

If you’re discriminated against at work there are ways to deal with it.

Employers have to follow the law on preventing discrimination at work.

## Other types of unfair treatment

You’re also protected from being treated unfairly because of:

- trade union membership or non-membership
- being a fixed-term or part-time worker

pages.summary:
Here’s a concise, actionable summary for your situation (England):

- You bought a veterinary service, so you’re entitled to care and skill that are reasonable. If the service wasn’t delivered with reasonable care and skill, you can complain.
- Steps to take:
  - First, use the vet’s own complaints procedure to try to resolve the issue.
  - If unresolved, you can contact the Veterinary Client Mediation Service for free, impartial mediation.
  - Consider legal action if mediation fails or isn’t appropriate. You usually must start negligence claims within 6 years.
- About possible outcomes:
  - They may correct the problem for free.
  - They may offer a full or partial refund if they can’t correct the problem.
  - If negligence is found, you may be entitled to compensation for extra costs or harm to your pet.
- Negligence vs. professional judgment:
  - Proving negligence means showing the standard of care wasn’t what a reasonable vet would provide. It can be hard; second opinions may help, though some vets may be reluctant to participate.
- Reporting misconduct:
  - If you suspect professional misconduct, you can report to the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons (RCVS). They can investigate and discipline the vet, but they do not award compensation.

Practical takeaways for your £2,700 knee replacement:
- Gather all fixed-cost quotes, invoices, and the consult discussion.
- Start with the vet’s complaints process; request a clear explanation of the charge and what you’re seeking (e.g., correction of issue, refund).
- If unsatisfied, contact the Veterinary Client Mediation Service.
- If you believe there was negligence, consider obtaining a second veterinary opinion and seek legal advice. You have up to 6 years for negligence claims; start earlier if possible.

If you’re unhappy with a service in England, you may be entitled to have the service redone or get a discount/refund under the Consumer Rights Act 2015. Key points:
- You can ask the trader to redo the service if possible, or seek a discount, especially if a redo isn’t possible, would take too long, or would be very inconvenient.
- If the service was originally agreed to with the expectation of reasonable care and skill, you’re entitled to remedies for problems that arise later (e.g., a broken item or poor workmanship). This can apply up to 6 years in England and Wales (and NI).
- Legally, you must be offered the chance to have the service redone before pursuing a refund/discount, unless a redo isn’t feasible.
- If the trader won’t fix it, you can discuss a price reduction or pursue dispute resolution options.
- For help, contact Citizens Advice (consumer service) for advice by phone or online chat.

This page provides England-focused guidance with references to the Consumer Rights Act 2015 and outlines steps to request a redo or discount and how to communicate your rights to the trader.

pages.summary:
If you’re in Manchester (Moston) and recently housed by HOST in another borough, you may still be eligible for homeless help or longer-term housing under UK guidance.

Key points from Citizens Advice guidance:
- You can apply to your local council for help if you’re legally homeless or have been threatened with homelessness within 8 weeks.
- Eligibility starts with your immigration status; check if you can apply for homeless help.
- If you’re threatened with homelessness, the council should assess and may help you stay in your home or find new housing.
- If you’re already homeless, the council will help you find a new home or consider emergency/longer-term housing.
- Length of help typically 8 weeks; this can extend if you’re threatened with homelessness and have a valid Section 8 notice.
- Longer-term housing depends on factors like whether you’re intentionally homeless and local connections (local “admission” rules) to the area.
- A local connection generally means you have ties to a council area (e.g., residence, family, work). If you lack a local connection in Manchester, the council may coordinate with other authorities but you still should get housing assistance; exceptions apply if safety/violence concerns exist.

What you should consider given your situation:
- Contact your current local council (the one covering Manchester/Moston) to verify if you’re legally homeless or threatened with homelessness and to start an eligibility assessment.
- Explain your housing history (HOST involvement, current shared housing, age 35) and any risk factors (violence, safety) that could affect local connection considerations.
- If you’re not considered locally connected to Manchester, ask about inter-borough arrangements and how that affects access to longer-term housing.
- If you’re not sure about your immigration status or eligibility, seek advice from Citizens Advice or your housing advisor.

If you want, I can tailor steps you can take next (who to call, what to ask, and draft a brief summary of your situation for a council appointment).

highlights:
Passing a tenancy to someone else - Citizens Advice

# Passing a tenancy to someone else

This advice applies to Scotland. See advice for See advice for England, See advice for Northern Ireland, See advice for Wales

## How to pass your tenancy on to someone else

Passing a tenancy to someone else is called assignation. The rules about when you can assign your tenancy depend on your tenancy type.

You can check what type of tenancy you have on the Shelter Scotland website.

If you need help with an assignation, you can get advice from your local Citizens Advice Bureau.

### If you rent from a local council or housing association

If you have a Scottish Secure Tenancy, you can assign the tenancy to anyone who has lived with you for the past 12 months. The property must have been their main home for that 12 months.

You must get the landlord’s permission in writing to assign your tenancy. Your landlord can only refuse if they have a good reason.

### If you rent from a private landlord

If you have a Private Residential Tenancy, you can only assign the tenancy to someone else if the tenancy agreement allows it, or the landlord agrees to it in writing.

## How to pass on a tenancy when someone dies

When a tenant dies the tenancy might pass to a partner, or sometimes a relative or carer. This is called succession.

The rules about when you can succeed a tenancy depend on the tenancy type. Succession rights are given by law. What a landlord says or writes in an agreement cannot change a right to succession.

Check your housing rights when someone you live with dies on the Shelter Scotland website.

To find out if you can succeed a tenancy, you can get advice from your local Citizens Advice Bureau.

- Succession rules are set by law and cannot be changed by a landlord’s agreement or a tenancy clause. Check your specific rights and eligibility with Shelter Scotland or Citizens Advice.

  - Check Shelter Scotland resources for your tenancy type and succession rights.
  - If you intend to remain, discuss with the landlord (and obtain any necessary written approvals) or explore succession rights through official guidance.

- The Private Housing (Tenancies) (Scotland) Act 2016 includes a provision allowing a resident carer to take over the tenancy if the sole tenant dies and no one else inherits under sections 67 or 68.
- Key conditions for a resident carer to become the tenant:
  - The carer is at least 16 years old at the time of the tenant’s death.
  - The carer was occupying the let property as their only or principal home at the time of the tenant’s death, and has done so continuously for at least 12 months ending with the tenant’s death.

- A “resident carer” is a person who provides care for the tenant or a member of the tenant’s family.

  1) Confirm eligibility: you’ve been the resident carer, occupying the home as your main residence for at least 12 months, and you’re at least 16.
  2) If you meet conditions and there is no other heir under sections 67/68, you may automatically become the tenant under the tenancy.
  3) Notify the landlord in writing about the change in occupancy status and your intention to become tenant, if required by the tenancy agreement.
  4) If there are complications (e.g., multiple potential successors or disputes about eligibility), seek advice.

Here’s a focused summary for your situation in Scotland, based on the Citizens Advice guidance “What to do after a death”:

- Register the death within 8 days (can be done at any registration office; see mygov.scot for details). As you live in the house, you’ll still need to register the death in person.

- Arranging the funeral: the funeral should be arranged by the person named in a will or declared by the deceased; there is no legal obligation to follow their stated wishes, but they are usually observed.

pages.title: Employment practices and data protection: monitoring workers | ICO
highlights:
Employment practices and data protection: monitoring workers | ICO

# Employment practices and data protection: monitoring workers

Due to changes made by the Data (Use and Access) Act, this guidance is under review and may be subject to change. The Plans for new and updated guidance page will tell you about which guidance will be updated and when this will happen.

Contents

Please give us your feedback about this guidance by filling in our survey.

This guidance discusses the monitoring of workers by employers, and how this interacts with data protection. It is primarily aimed at employers. The guidance aims to:

- help provide greater regulatory certainty;
- protect workers’ data protection rights; and
- help employers to build trust with workers, customers and service users.

The guidance provides clarity and practical advice to help employers to comply with the UK General Data Protection Regulation (UK GDPR) and the Data Protection Act 2018 (DPA 2018). It assumes some knowledge of data protection, but provides links to other pieces of key data protection guidance, if you want to find out more information.

We use the term ‘worker’ throughout this guidance only to refer to someone who performs work for an organisation. Business models have changed in the last decade, with the rise of the gig economy. This guidance captures these relationships too. It is aimed at all circumstances where there is an employment relationship or otherwise a relationship between an organisation and a person who performs work for the organisation, regardless of the nature of the contract.

To help you understand the law and good practice as clearly as possible, this guidance says what organisations must, should, and could do to comply.

## Legislative requirements

Must refers to legislative requirements.

## Good practice

Should does not refer to a legislative requirement, but what we expect you to do to comply effectively with the law. You should do this unless there is a good reason not to. If you choose to take a different approach, you must be able to demonstrate that this approach also complies with the law.

Could refers to an option or example that you could consider to help you to comply effectively. There are likely to be various other ways you could comply.
pages.summary:
Summary tailored to your question:

- The ICO guidance on monitoring workers explains what employers can and cannot do with employee data under UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018. It covers monitoring in all work relationships, including gig economy and third-party apps.
- Key point: Use of a third-party workplace app is permissible if it complies with data protection laws. Employers should have a legitimate basis for processing, be transparent about what is monitored, and implement data minimization, security, and retention practices.
- If you’re in Scotland, UK GDPR applies the same principles; there isn’t a separate rule just because you’re in Scotland.

Practical steps:
- Check what data the app collects, why, how long it’s kept, who has access, and where data is stored.
- Ensure you’ve been informed about monitoring purposes and have access to a privacy notice.
- If you have concerns about specific data processing or if you believe data protection rights are breached (e.g., unnecessary monitoring, data sharing without justification), you can raise concerns with your employer, your organization’s data protection officer, or file a complaint with the ICO.
- If you’ve used the app for 6+ years, verify any changes in policy, data retention, and third-party data sharing since you started.

For precise guidance, refer to ICO’s “Employment practices and data protection: monitoring workers” page and UK GDPR/DPA 2018 guidance. If you want, I can tailor steps based on your exact role and the app in question.

# Compensation after an accident or injury

# Using a solicitor or a claims company

You cannot usually get legal aid for personal injury cases.

A solicitor should advise you on costs before you agree to hire them.

Get advice from Citizens Advice on what’s involved in taking legal action and how much it will cost you.

## Claims companies

Businesses known as claims companies can help you find a solicitor.

Most claims handlers are not solicitors, and so will not be able to represent you in court.

Check that a claims company is registered.

## ‘No win, no fee’ deals

If you use a ‘no win, no fee’ agreement, you will only have to pay the solicitor’s fee if you win the case.

You may still have to pay for some other costs, like:

- fees to pay for experts
- court fees
- travelling expenses

If you lose, you will also have to pay for:

- the other side’s legal costs
- other expenses and charges, such as fees for witnesses

The solicitor may charge a fee for winning the case.

# Check your insurance policies

You may already have insurance to pay for the legal costs of making a claim for compensation. You can:

- check your insurance policies (such as motor, home contents or holiday insurance policies) to see if they include ‘legal expenses insurance’

If you’re not insured, you could take out insurance after the incident to protect yourself against a large legal bill.

If you win, you may be able to get some of the costs back from the losing side.

Some insurance companies will not insure you if they think you’re unlikely to succeed, and some policies are very expensive.

# Write a letter, complain or try mediation

You can get compensation by taking legal action, but it could cost you money and you may not win your case against the person or organisation to blame.

## Writing a letter or making a complaint

If it’s not a serious injury, you may be able to solve the issue by writing a letter or making a complaint - use the complaints procedure if there is one.

Explain what went wrong and tell them how much compensation you want or how they can make up for the injury.

## Using mediation

You might be able to negotiate a settlement using mediation. This is when an impartial professional (the mediator) helps both sides work out an agreement. It’s confidential and usually quicker and cheaper than going to court.

Summary:

- The page provides CPS prosecution guidance on communications offences, covering acts where someone communicates something by any means (electronic or otherwise).
- Primary focus: offences under Malicious Communications Act 1988 (MCA 1988), Communications Act 2003 (CA 2003), and offences in Part 10 of the Online Safety Act 2023 (OSA 2023).

- Notes on related misconduct: communications offences can coincide with other misconduct (e.g., assault, harassment, stalking, public order, sexual offences, contempt of court, public justice, coercive control).
- Charging and decision-making: prosecutors should consider appropriate charge choices under the relevant statutes; seek guidance up to Chief Crown Prosecutor (CCP) for complex issues.
- Key offences highlighted:

- Evidence considerations: for MCA 1988 and CA 2003, proof of receipt is not required; only that the message was sent. However, victim evidence about offence-caused fear or gross offense can be relevant to the assessment of the offence’s quality, depending on other evidence.
- Practical implications: prosecutors must assess whether communications caused fear, offense, or apprehension; consider victim involvement in trials accordingly.
- The guidance emphasizes alignment with the Code for Crown Prosecutors and internal referral processes for complex charging decisions.

All the information and guidance you need about making a complaint about the police.

We oversee the police complaints system in England and Wales, however most complaints are handled by the relevant police force. Each force has a department that makes sure that complaints are dealt with appropriately, these are usually called professional standards departments.

- Estimate the estate’s value for Inheritance Tax, even if no tax is due.
- Determine if the estate is an “excepted estate” (full details to HMRC may not be required).
- If IHT is due, pay it first and obtain a unique HMRC code needed to apply; for excepted estates, you can apply straight away.
- You must report estate value as part of the probate application using an online IHT checker (provides part of the required values).
- If full details to HMRC are required, complete form IHT400 within 12 months of death.
- If IHT is due, payment is usually required before probate; payments can be recovered from the estate.
- Gather required documents: death certificate (with certain conditions) and original will (if any).
- Steps include valuing the estate, checking IHT, and then applying for probate, followed by settling debts/taxes and distributing assets in line with the will or law.

Skip to main content

# IHTM12111 - Succession: intestacy: rules in England and Wales: summary of the main rules of intestacy

If the deceased died without making a Will the whole of their estate will pass under the rules of intestacy.

If the deceased made a Will but the Will did not effectively dispose of all their estate this will be a partial intestacy (IHTM12128). The property that was not disposed of by the Will passes under the rules of intestacy.

The way in which an estate is distributed will depend on whether the deceased was married or in a civil partnership and which of their relatives are still alive when they die.

## Surviving spouse or civil partner

The Inheritance and Trustees’ Powers Act 2014, which came into force on 1 October 2014, made amendments to the intestacy rules where the deceased left a surviving spouse or civil partner.

## For deaths on or after 1 October 2014

If the deceased was survived by a spouse or civil partner they will take:

- The personal chattels, a fixed net sum (statutory legacy) and an absolute interest in one half of the residue. The issue take the other half share on statutory trust.
- The whole estate passing on intestacy if there was no issue.

Top of page

## For deaths before 1 October 2014

If the deceased was survived by a spouse or civil partner they will take:

- The chattels, a statutory legacy and a share of the residue (IHTM12121) - if there were any issue (children), parent, brother, sister or issue of brother or sister.
- All the estate passing by intestacy (IHTM12121) - if there were no issue (children), parent, brother, sister or issue of brother or sister.

The rest of the estate will be distributed to the issue or other relatives.

Top of page

## Issue

If there was no surviving spouse or civil partner but the deceased had children the estate would be distributed amongst them (IHTM12124).

Top of page

## Other relatives

If there was no surviving spouse or civil partner and no children the estate would be distributed amongst the deceased’s other relatives (IHTM12125).

Top of page

## No relatives

If no living relatives can be found the estate will pass to the Crown as bona vacantia (IHTM12126).

This page outlines Part 57 of the Civil Procedure Rules (CPR) in England and Wales, which governs matters related to probate, inheritance, presumption of death, and the guardianship of missing persons. It details:

- Scope and definitions for Part 57.
- I. Probate claims: general rules, initiating a probate claim, service/defence, lodging testamentary documents, revocation of grants, statements of case, counterclaims, probate-related dismissals.
- II. Rectification of Wills: procedures to rectify wills.
- III. Substitution/removal of personal representatives: process for changing personal representatives.
- IV. Claims under the Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975: scope, High Court proceedings, and procedural steps for section 1 claims (including filing requirements and evidence standards).
- V. Proceedings under the presumption of death: relevant rules (Reference to relevant sections and procedures within Part 57).

Key points relevant to a typical England-based will challenge or disputes over inheritance:
- If disputing a will or an estate, you would use probate-related rules under Part 57, including filing statements of case, and potentially bringing a claim under the Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975 (Section 1).
- Defendants with a potential interest in the grant or estate must consider filing a counterclaim.
- For claims under the 1975 Act, there are specific procedural steps (use of Form Part 8, accompanying evidence, and statutory requirements) and special provisions if no grant has been issued.

If you need guidance tailored to contesting a will or pursuing provision under the 1975 Act (e.g., intestacy scenarios or Citizen Advice-style guidance), I can extract the exact procedural steps from Part 57 and map them to common scenarios.

Summary:

- This guidance (England) from Citizens Advice explains section 21 evictions for private tenants and how the process works in practice.
- Key timing: a valid section 21 notice can lead to a court possession order; the landlord must apply to the court, and eviction can proceed only with court involvement and, if needed, a warrant for eviction. Illegal eviction remains a risk if the landlord tries to remove you without a court order.

- What to do next: If you believe your notice is valid, prepare for potential court proceedings; if not valid, seek advice to challenge the eviction and remedy issues (deposit protection, prescribed information).

- Prescribed information: Landlords must provide this paperwork; late provision or returning the deposit can affect eviction rights.

highlights:
Tenancy deposit protection: Overview - GOV.UK

Skip to main content

# Tenancy deposit protection

Skip contents

# Overview

Your landlord must put your deposit in a government-approved tenancy deposit scheme (TDP) if you rent your home on an assured shorthold tenancy that started after 6 April 2007. In England and Wales your deposit can be registered with:

- Deposit Protection Service
- MyDeposits- including deposits that were held by Capita
- Tenancy Deposit Scheme

If you do not rent your home on an assured shorthold tenancy, your landlord can accept valuable items (for example a car or watch) as a deposit instead of money. The items will not be protected by a scheme.

They make sure you’ll get your deposit back if you:

- meet the terms of your tenancy agreement
- do not damage the property
- pay your rent and bills

Your landlord or letting agent must put your deposit in the scheme within 30 days of getting it.

## If you’re in Scotland or Northern Ireland

There are separate TDP schemes in Scotland and Northern Ireland. Find out about:

TDP schemes in Scotland

TDP schemes in Northern Ireland

## At the end of your tenancy

Your landlord must return your deposit within 10 days of you both agreeing how much you’ll get back.

If you’re in a dispute with your landlord, then your deposit will be protected in the TDP scheme until the issue is sorted out.

## Holding deposits

Your landlord does not have to protect a holding deposit (money you pay to ‘hold’ a property before an agreement is signed). Once you become a tenant, the holding deposit becomes a deposit, which they must protect.

## Deposits made by a third party

Your landlord must use a TDP scheme even if your deposit is paid by someone else, such as a rent deposit scheme or your parents.

highlights:
Private renting: Your rights and responsibilities - GOV.UK

Skip to main content

# Private renting

Skip contents

# Your rights and responsibilities

You have certain rights and responsibilities if you’re a tenant in privately rented property.

## Your rights

As a tenant, you have the right to:

- live in a property that’s safe and in a good state of repair
- have your deposit returned when the tenancy ends - and in some circumstances have your deposit protected
- challenge excessively high charges
- know who your landlord is
- live in the property undisturbed
- see an Energy Performance Certificate for the property
- be protected from unfair eviction and unfair rent

If you have a tenancy agreement, it should be fair and comply with the law.

If you do not know who your landlord is, write to the person or company you pay rent to. Your landlord can be fined If they do not give you this information within 21 days.

## Your responsibilities

You should give your landlord access to the property to inspect it or carry out repairs. Your landlord has to give you at least 24 hours’ notice and visit at a reasonable time of day, unless it’s an emergency and they need immediate access.

You must also:

- take good care of the property, for example turn off the water at the mains if you’re away in cold weather
- pay the agreed rent, even if repairs are needed or you’re in dispute with your landlord
- pay other charges as agreed with the landlord, for example Council Tax or utility bills
- repair or pay for any damage caused by you, your family or friends
- only sublet a property if the tenancy agreement or your landlord allows it

Your landlord has the right to take legal action to evict you if you do not meet your responsibilities.

### If your landlord lives outside the UK

Contact HM Revenue and Customs(HMRC) if your landlord lives outside the UK and you pay £100 or more a week in rent directly to them.

You may have to deduct tax from your rent under HMRC’s ‘ non-resident landlord scheme’.

Skip to main content

# Avoid unfair terms in sales contracts

Skip contents

# Unfair consumer contracts

You cannot enforce unfair terms in a consumer contract, or unfair consumer notices, for example, signs on a shop wall or in a car park.

You can never enforce terms or notices that try to avoid your responsibility for:

- death
- injury
- faulty goods
- goods that are not as described
- selling goods that are not yours to sell

You might not be able to enforce terms or notices if they try to avoid your responsibility in other ways, such as for:

- delays
- unsatisfactory services
- not doing what was agreed

Your contract terms might also be unfair if the contract is significantly weighted in your favour, for example:

- by providing for excessive cancellation charges and automatic loss of all upfront payments
- by creating unbalanced rights, for example, being able to cancel a contract at any time, but requiring the customer to give 3 months’ notice
- by allowing you to increase the agreed price at a later date

Your contract will not be unfair just because it sets a price that’s higher than another business charges.

Read more about how to write fair contracts.

Contracts must be written in plain language to avoid being misleading and unfair.

## If a customer complains

It’s up to the courts to decide if a term in your contract or wording in your notices is unfair.

You can be taken to court by the Competition and Markets Authority or a local trading standards office to stop you using unfair terms or notices.

Consumers can also take legal action themselves to challenge unfair terms or notices.

highlights:
Consumer Rights Act 2015

- Skip to main content

Back to full view

# Consumer Rights Act 2015

- Previous: Provision
- Next: Provision

#### 62Requirement for contract terms and notices to be fairU.K.

This section has no associated Explanatory Notes

(1)An unfair term of a consumer contract is not binding on the consumer.

(2)An unfair consumer notice is not binding on the consumer.

(3)This does not prevent the consumer from relying on the term or notice if the consumer chooses to do so.

(4)A term is unfair if, contrary to the requirement of good faith, it causes a significant imbalance in the parties' rights and obligations under the contract to the detriment of the consumer.

(5)Whether a term is fair is to be determined—

(a)taking into account the nature of the subject matter of the contract, and

(b)by reference to all the circumstances existing when the term was agreed and to all of the other terms of the contract or of any other contract on which it depends.

(6)A notice is unfair if, contrary to the requirement of good faith, it causes a significant imbalance in the parties' rights and obligations to the detriment of the consumer.

(7)Whether a notice is fair is to be determined—

(a)taking into account the nature of the subject matter of the notice, and

(b)by reference to all the circumstances existing when the rights or obligations to which it relates arose and to the terms of any contract on which it depends.

(8)This section does not affect the operation of—

(a)section 31 (exclusion of liability: goods contracts),

(b)section 47 (exclusion of liability: digital content contracts),

(c)section 57 (exclusion of liability: services contracts), or

(d)section 65 (exclusion of negligence liability).

Commencement Information

Summary:

- Section 62 of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 concerns fairness of contract terms and notices in consumer contracts.
- Key points:
  - Unfair terms or unfair notices are not binding on the consumer.
  - The consumer may still choose to rely on the term/notice if they wish.
  - A term or notice is unfair if, contrary to the requirement of good faith, it causes a significant imbalance in the parties’ rights and obligations to the detriment of the consumer.
  - Fairness is assessed by: the nature of the subject matter and all circumstances at the time the term was agreed, along with other terms the contract depends on (for terms) or the surrounding rights/obligations when the notice arises (for notices).
  - The section does not override exclusions of liability listed in sections 31, 47, 57 or 65.
- Commencement: Section 62 came into force on 1 October 2015.

This blog explains what consumer law means for deposit and cancellation fees, and how you can make sure you’re being treated fairly.
...
Under consumer law, businesses must make sure their terms are fair. If a term is considered unfair by a court, then it can’t be enforced against the customer even if they have signed up to it. It is particularly worth looking out for unfair terms with deposit and cancellation fees.
...
Businesses are entitled to ask customers to pay a fee if they cancel – or to keep some of an upfront deposit – to cover their losses. But the amount they keep must be in proportion to what they are actually losing as a result of a cancellation.
...
Terms and conditions that don’t follow this approach – for example, where the business keeps a large upfront deposit which bears no relation to its losses – are likely to be unfair. As a general rule, deposits should only be a small percentage of the total cost.
...
In practice this means that if you cancel a booking and a business resells it, you should be entitled to some money back. Travel firms can either use a case-by-case system, where people are refunded if and when a replacement booking is made, or they can have general terms and conditions based on how likely it is that they will be able to resell any cancelled bookings as the date of the booking approaches.
...

highlights:
Dismissal: your rights: Overview - GOV.UK

Skip to main content

# Dismissal: your rights

Skip contents

# Overview

Dismissal is when your employer ends your employment - they do not always have to give you notice.

If you’re dismissed, your employer must show they’ve:

- a valid reason that they can justify
- acted reasonably in the circumstances

They must also:

- be consistent - for example, not dismiss you for doing something that they let other employees do
- have investigated the situation fully before dismissing you - for example, if a complaint was made about you

If you’re a part-time or fixed-term worker, you cannot be treated less favourably than a full-time or permanent employee.

## Notice period

You must be given at least the notice stated in your contract or the statutory minimum notice period, whichever is longer.

There are some situations where you can be dismissed immediately- for example, for violence.

## Getting your dismissal in writing

You have the right to ask for a written statement from your employer giving the reasons why you’ve been dismissed if you’re an employee and have completed 2 years’ service.

Your employer must supply the statement within 14 days of you asking for it.

Your employer must give you a written statement if you’re dismissed while you are on Statutory Maternity Leave. You get this:

- even if you’ve not asked for one
- regardless of how long you’ve worked for your employer

Speak to your employer or check your employment status if you’re unsure of your employment status.

Skip to main content

# Redundancy: your rights

Skip contents

# Overview

Redundancy is a form of dismissal from your job. It happens when employers need to reduce their workforce.

If you’re being made redundant, you might be eligible for certain things, including:

- redundancy pay
- a notice period
- a consultation with your employer
- the option to move into a different job
- time off to find a new job

You also have specific rights if your employer is insolvent.

You must be selected for redundancy in a fair way, for example because of your level of experience or capability to do the job.

You cannot be selected because of age, gender, or if you’re disabled or pregnant. If you are, this could be classed as an unfair dismissal.

## Get advice

You can get advice on redundancy from Acas (Advisory, Conciliation and Arbitration Service) or Citizens Advice.

Summary for "Statutory redundancy pay" (GOV.UK)

- Eligibility: Entitled to statutory redundancy pay if you’re an employee and have worked for the current employer for 2 or more years.
- Calculation:
  - 0.5 week’s pay for each full year under age 22
  - 1 week’s pay for each full year aged 22–40
  - 1.5 weeks’ pay for each full year aged 41 or older
  - Length of service cap: 20 years
  - Weekly pay is the average earnings over the 12 weeks before the redundancy notice
- Caps (as of 6 April 2026): weekly pay cap £751; maximum statutory redundancy pay £22,530. Earlier dates have lower caps.
- Timing: You have 6 months from job end to claim.
- Exclusions: Not entitled if the employer keeps you on, or offers suitable alternative work you refuse without good reason; dismissal for misconduct; certain groups (e.g., former dock workers, crown servants, police, armed forces, apprentices not employees at end, a domestic servant in employer’s immediate family).
- Furlough: If you were paid during coronavirus furlough, the calculation uses what you would have earned normally.
- Short-term/temporary lay-offs: You can claim if you’re eligible and laid off without pay or for under half a week, for more than 4 consecutive weeks or more than 6 non-consecutive weeks in 13 weeks. Need to notify employer in writing within specific timeframes; employer has 7 days to reject after receipt, else your claim proceeds. Claim may be rejected if regular work would resume within 4 weeks and continue for at least 13 weeks.

pages.summary:
Summary:
This Acas page explains what constitutes bullying at work in the UK. Bullying is unwanted behavior that is offensive, intimidating, or undermines a person, and can be a regular pattern or a one-off incident. It may occur face-to-face or online, at work or in work-related contexts, and isn’t always obvious to others. Examples include constant criticism, spreading rumours, belittling in meetings, assigning excessive workloads, exclusion from team activities, or posting humiliating content on social media. Bullying can target anyone, including managers (upward bullying).

Legal context:
There is no specific law defining bullying. However, bullying can amount to discrimination under the Equality Act 2010 if it relates to protected characteristics or beliefs, with four main types of discrimination: direct, indirect, harassment, and victimisation. Even non-discriminatory bullying can raise legal issues (e.g., constructive dismissal if it leads to resignation).

Employer/employee duties:
- Employers have a duty of care to protect workers from harm and should prevent bullying, investigate complaints promptly, and take them seriously.
- Employees have the right to work without bullying and to expect trust and confidence in their employer; both parties should treat each other with respect and follow reasonable instructions.

Support:
Acas provides guidance, a helpline, and free e-learning on bullying and harassment. No specific links to further resources are included in the extras.

pages.summary:
Acas guidance on sick leave for England covers how employers should handle sickness absence, including bullying or harassment related to sickness. Key points:

- Eligibility and types of leave: Sick leave can be for both physical and mental health; employees may need to self-certify for up to 7 calendar days and provide a fit note after that.
- Reporting and documentation: Employees tell their employer when sick; after 7 days, a fit note from a healthcare professional is required.
- Sick pay: Employees may have a right to sick pay, depending on contract and policy.
- Contact during sickness: Employers and employees should agree an appropriate level of contact; mutual respect is important, especially in harassment/bullying contexts.
- Returning to work: Return-to-work discussions and potential phased returns help ensure readiness and support.
- Mental health focus: Mental health conditions are treated with the same seriousness as physical illnesses, and work-related causes should be investigated and addressed if applicable.
- Workplace harassment: If bullying/harassment is influencing sickness or workplace wellbeing, employers should address the issue promptly and take steps to resolve it.

Relation to unpaid wages: Sick leave pay may be paid or unpaid depending on the contract and statutory entitlements; the guidance emphasizes rights and duties but does not replace contract terms or specify universal unpaid wages beyond statutory sick pay where applicable. For detailed entitlements, consult the contract, Acas, and GOV.UK guidance.

pages.summary:
ACAS guidance on sick pay entitlement in the UK:

- Sick pay basics: If you’re off sick, you may be entitled to sick pay, with both physical and mental health illnesses covered.
- Contract checks: Your contract should specify how much sick pay you get, how long it lasts, and any rules for using sick pay.
- Statutory sick pay (SSP): If eligible, your employer must pay at least SSP.
- Company/occupational sick pay: Employers may offer more than SSP through discretionary or contractual schemes. If discretionary, it must be stated in writing (contracts or company policies) and must avoid discrimination and treat part-time workers fairly.
- Discretionary policy rules: Policies should not discriminate against protected characteristics (e.g., disability) and should apply equally to part-time and full-time workers.
- What if there’s nothing in writing: You can ask your manager or HR for the policy, or talk to a trade union representative if applicable.
- Sick pay and work-related sickness: The same sick pay rules apply to illnesses caused by work unless the contract or policy says otherwise.
- Probation: Statutory sick pay eligibility isn’t affected by probation; you’re entitled to SSP if you qualify.

Overall, assess your contract for the exact sick pay terms, know your SSP rights, and check any discretionary company sick pay policies for terms and nondiscrimination guarantees. For broader issues like workplace bullying/harassment, ACAS and Citizens Advice provide separate guidance on rights and remedies in England.

# How to appeal a penalty charge notice

You may be able to appeal to an independent tribunal against a penalty charge notice (PCN) if you think it’s wrong.

This includes any PCN issued in England or Wales for:

- parking
- breaking traffic rules while moving (‘moving traffic contraventions’), for example driving in a bus lane when you should not
- not paying the Dartford Crossing, London congestion or low emissions zone charge on time

There are different ways to appeal in Scotland and appeal in Northern Ireland.

Before you can appeal, you must make a formal challenge(called a ‘representation’).

## When to appeal

You must wait to find out the outcome of your formal challenge. If it’s rejected, you’ll get a ‘notice of rejection’ in the post.

After you’ve received the notice, you have 28 days to make an appeal.

## How to appeal

Find out how to appeal to:

- London Tribunals if your PCN was issued in London
- the Traffic Penalty Tribunal if your PCN was issued outside London, in England or Wales - this includes PCNs from Dart Charge

If your appeal is successful the PCN will be cancelled and you will not have to pay anything.

This GOV.UK guide explains how to appeal a penalty charge notice (PCN) in England or Wales, including parking, moving traffic contraventions (e.g., bus lanes), and charges like Dartford Crossing or London congestion/Low Emission Zone if paid late. Before appealing, you must lodge a formal challenge (a “representation”). If your challenge is rejected, you’ll receive a notice of rejection, after which you have 28 days to appeal. Appeals are handled by the London Tribunals (for London-issued PCNs) or the Traffic Penalty Tribunal (for non-London PCNs in England/Wales, including Dart Charge). If the appeal succeeds, the PCN is cancelled and you owe nothing.

Key points for your likely needs:
- Appeals can be made for parking, moving traffic, and late payments of certain charges.
- Start with a formal challenge; only after a rejection can you appeal.
- Timeframe: 28 days from the notice of rejection to appeal.
- Tribunal options depend on where the PCN was issued: London Tribunals (London) or Traffic Penalty Tribunal (elsewhere in England/Wales).

- Penalty points and disqualification: Accumulating 12 or more penalty points within 3 years triggers disqualification (minimum 6 months; longer if previously disqualified). Courts can disqualify for any penalty-point offence, usually 1 week to a few months.

Summary:
The GOV.UK page explains how to challenge (appeal) a parking ticket or penalty charge notice (PCN) in England. Key points:
- You have 28 days to challenge a PCN. If you challenge within 14 days and it’s rejected, you may pay only 50% of the fine.
- There are different challenge routes depending on ticket type:
  - Local council PCN on the spot: informal challenge with the council.
  - Local council PCN by post: formal challenge (representation) with the council.
  - Dart Charge PCN: a representation with Dart Charge.
  - Red route PCN, Congestion charge PCN, Low Emission Zone PCN: representation with Transport for London (TfL).
- Informal challenges (if accepted) mean you won’t pay the fine.
- If an informal challenge is rejected, you’ll receive a notice to owner with instructions for paying or making a formal challenge.
- For formal challenges (representations), you must detail your reasons and provide supporting evidence; acceptance means no payment.
- If a formal challenge is rejected, you’ll get a notice of rejection with 28 days to pay or appeal to an independent tribunal. Non-payment can lead to a late penalty (charge certificate) and you may need to go to a magistrates’ court.
- For private parking tickets, check the issuer and follow their process. If rejected, you can appeal to an accredited trade association (POPLA for BPA members; IAS for IPC members).

pages.title: Road Traffic - Summary Offences
highlights:
Where a defendant raises exceptional hardship as a reason for not being disqualified under the repeated offence provisions of section 35 RTOA 1988 it is appropriate for the prosecutor to question the defendant. This should be done with the approval of the court and in order to assist in determining the question of disqualification.
...
### Failing to Stop/Report an Accident
...
Section 170(2) RTA 1988 provides that the driver of the motor vehicle must stop following an accident and, if required to do so by any person having reasonable grounds for so requiring, give his name and address, the name and address of the owner of the vehicle and the identification marks of the vehicle. The duty to stop means to stop sufficiently long enough to exchange the particulars above: (Lee v Knapp [1966] 3 All ER 961).
...
Section 170(3) RTA 1988 places an obligation on the driver, if they do not give their name and address under subsection (2) above, to report the accident to a police constable or police station as soon as reasonably practicable and in any case within 24 hours. The duty to report means "as soon as reasonably practicable": (Bulman v Bennett [1974] RTR 1). It does not mean the driver has 24 hours within which to report the collision.
...
When the evidence reveals a failure to comply with both subsections (2) and (3), proceedings should be brought for both offences. Failing to stop is usually viewed as the more serious of the two offences; it may be appropriate to accept a guilty plea to that offence in many cases.
...
There is no mutual recognition of penalty points between the jurisdictions, so the UK court cannot take into account Irish penalty points, for totting up purposes. However, the court has a wide discretion, in considering whether to impose discretionary disqualifications in the UK, to consider all mitigating or aggravating factors. The court therefore may consider the driver's licence history generally.
pages.summary:
Summary:
This CPS guidance covers road traffic offences under the Road Traffic Act 1988 related to exceptional hardship and totting up, plus specific duties after accidents. Key points include:
- Exceptional hardship as a reason not to be disqualified under section 35 RTOA 1988: prosecutors should question the defendant about exceptional hardship with court approval to help determine disqualification.
- Failing to stop or report an accident: under Section 170(2) RTA 1988 the driver must stop, exchange name/address and vehicle details; if not given, Section 170(3) requires reporting to police as soon as reasonably practicable, and in any case within 24 hours. “As soon as reasonably practicable” is required and does not permit a full 24-hour window to report.
- If evidence shows a failure to comply with both subsections (2) and (3), proceedings should be brought for both offences; failing to stop is generally the more serious, and guilty pleas may be accepted for that offence in many cases.
- There is no mutual recognition of penalty points between the UK and Irish jurisdictions for totting up; UK courts cannot rely on Irish points. However, UK courts may consider overall licence history and all mitigating or aggravating factors when deciding discretionary disqualifications.

Practical implication for the user’s query: The guidance explains how exceptional hardship is considered in totting-up cases, and clarifies duties to stop and to report after accidents, including timing requirements and how these affect prosecutions and potential disqualification. It confirms there is no cross-border (UK-Ireland) mutual points recognition for totting up, but UK courts may weigh broader licence history.

# Individual Voluntary Arrangements

An Individual Voluntary Arrangement (IVA) is an agreement with your creditors to pay all or part of your debts. You agree to make regular payments to an insolvency practitioner, who will divide this money between your creditors.

An IVA can give you more control of your assets than bankruptcy.

MoneyHelper has information about where to get free debt advice.

## Get an Individual Voluntary Arrangement (IVA)

Use an insolvency practitioner to get an IVA.

Your insolvency practitioner works out what you can afford to repay and how long the IVA lasts. You’ll have to give details about your financial situation, for example your assets, debts, income and creditors.

Your insolvency practitioner will contact your creditors. The IVA will start if the creditors holding 75% of your debts agree to it. It will apply to all your creditors, including any who disagreed to it.

An IVA will stop your creditors taking action against you for your debts.

## Costs

There are usually 2 fees:

- a set up fee
- a handling fee each time you make a payment

Make sure you know how much it’s going to cost before asking an insolvency practitioner to act for you.

## Your responsibilities

Your IVA can be cancelled by the insolvency practitioner if you do not keep up your repayments. The insolvency practitioner can make you bankrupt.

You may still be able to keep your business running, if you have one.

### Public records

Your IVA will be added to the Individual Insolvency Register. It’s removed 3 months after the IVA ends.

# Options for dealing with your debts

Skip contents

# Overview

If you owe people money (your ‘creditors’) you can make arrangements to pay your debts. Your options depend on the amount of money and assets you have.

## Where you can get help

Speak to a debt adviser to get help choosing the best way to deal with your debt.

MoneyHelper has information about debt management and free debt advisory services.

## Paying off your debts

You can pay your debts in instalments by setting up:

- a Debt Management Plan which is an agreement with your creditors managed by a financial company
- an Administration Order when you’ve had a county court judgment (CCJ) or a High Court judgment (HCJ) against you for debts under £5,000
- an Individual Voluntary Arrangement which is managed by an insolvency practitioner

You can also get temporary protection from your creditors through the‘Breathing Space’ scheme, while still making repayments. You’ll need to apply through a debt advisor.

In Scotland you can arrange a Debt Payment Programme from the Debt Arrangement Scheme.

You may also have the option of reaching an informal agreement with your creditors.

## If you cannot pay off your debt

You can apply for a Debt Relief Order or Bankruptcy Order if you cannot pay your debts because you do not have enough money or assets you can sell.

If you cannot pay off your debts, you can be made bankrupt.

Summary:
Citizens Advice explains what bailiffs (enforcement agents) can and cannot seize for debt in England. Key points:

- What bailiffs can take: belongings you own or jointly own (e.g., electrical items, jewelry, vehicle). They can also list items on a controlled goods agreement.
- Inside the home: they can only enter with permission; you can refuse entry to keep them out.
- Exempt items and limits: bailiffs cannot take items that belong to someone else (including your children), items needed for work or study up to £1,350, a Motability vehicle, or a vehicle with a Blue Badge. They cannot take items you need for basic domestic needs.
- Third-party and finance rules: they cannot usually take goods you’re paying for on certain finance agreements; if unsure, check with the lender.
- What to do if they overstep: if they take or list exempt or third-party goods, you should complain within 7 days; the bailiff must respond within 10 days.
- If items belong to someone else or are “exempt goods,” gather evidence and contact the bailiff to resolve.
- If they’re attempting to seize something that isn’t theirs or is exempt, you have grounds to challenge and recover the item.

Useful for: understanding your rights under English debt collection law, including exemptions, protection of work/study items up to £1,350, and the process for complaints. If you need specifics on a particular item or situation, consult Citizens Advice or GOV.UK guidance directly.

Summary:
The GOV.UK guidance explains how to enforce a money judgment in England if the debtor doesn’t pay, including using bailiffs (warrant of control) and Money Claim Online. Key points:
- You can request the court to collect payment from the debtor after a court order, but a court fee is required.
- If the debtor has a Breathing Space (temporary protection from creditors), enforcement cannot proceed until that ends and you’ve clarified your obligations to the court.
- To send bailiffs, apply for a warrant of control. Bailiffs will demand payment within 7 days and may visit the debtor’s home or business to seize eligible assets to satisfy the debt.

Summary:
- England-specific guidance from Citizens Advice on bailiffs (enforcement agents) rights and limits.
- Bailiffs can seize and sell your belongings only if you don’t arrange payment or breach a controlled goods agreement.
- Goods are usually sold at auction; proceeds go to the debt and bailiff fees. You still owe any shortfall.
- You’ll receive a notice of sale at least 7 days before the auction (excluding the 7-day period itself). If notice is less than 7 days, they cannot proceed.
- You can recover items if the sale is invalid or you negotiate a payment plan with your creditor.
- Bailiffs must provide:
  - A written estimate of items’ value before the sale; you can correct undervaluations.
  - A list after the sale detailing what was taken and the sale outcome.

pages.summary:
Summary:
The Citizens Advice guide explains the rights and limits of bailiffs (enforcement agents) in England and how to handle encounters at your home or business. Key points:

- Bailiffs can only try to enter between 6am and 9pm; you can keep them out by locking doors and using a locked porch.
- They may attempt entry for certain debts, but they cannot normally force entry without a locksmith; they must use 'reasonable force' and cannot break doors.
- For some debts (e.g., county court or High Court judgments) they may have the right to force entry to a business, but not to a private home.
- If they are just debt collectors (not bailiffs), they do not have the same powers; you can ask them to leave.
- If you let them in and can’t pay immediately, you may enter a 'controlled goods agreement' (a repayment plan with added bailiff fees).
- You have the right to talk to them through a closed door and to verify the debt is yours; if it isn’t, contact their head office.
- Do not be pressured to pay on the doorstep; refusing entry is allowed, and you should arrange payment or seek advice promptly to avoid extra fees.
- If you miss an agreement, a notice of intention to re-enter may be issued, allowing entry with a locksmith but not door braking.

This page emphasizes knowing your rights, avoiding coercion, and acting quickly to prevent additional fees.

Summary:
If someone owes you money and a court has ordered payment, you can apply for a warrant of control (bailiff enforcement) to recover the debt. The enforcement agent may seize goods owned by the defendant (or jointly owned) to raise money, after covering removal, storage, and sale costs. They will target items likely to fetch enough to cover costs; they cannot seize items the defendant needs for work, essential household items, leased/rented/hire-purchase items, or assets not owned by the defendant. Commonly seized items include second-hand furniture and other items with resale value.

- You must have a court order; apply for a warrant of control (N323 form).
- Enforcement agents may take goods to satisfy the debt, but only if sale proceeds will cover costs.
- Certain items cannot be taken (work-related tools, essential items, leased/hired goods, etc.).
- Before applying, seek legal advice (solicitor, law centre, Citizens Advice).

Summary:

- Topic: Controlled goods agreements with bailiffs (enforcement agents) in England.
- Key concept: If you can’t pay a debt in full, you may agree to a controlled goods agreement with the bailiff to avoid further removal of belongings. This sets a repayment plan for the debt.
- What happens: Bailiffs compile an inventory of belongings they have taken control of; these items must be listed and can only be those covered by the agreement.
- Your rights and steps:
  - You can propose a repayment plan you can realistically afford; use a budget to prove what you can pay.
  - Do not agree to payments you cannot sustain; the bailiff should not pressure you into unaffordable terms.
  - Keep to the repayment plan; missing payments allows the bailiff to remove and sell listed items.

  - If you breach the agreement, the bailiff can return to remove items to sell.

# Running a limited company: your responsibilities

# Directors’ responsibilities

As a director of a limited company, you must:

- follow the company’s rules, shown in its articles of association
- keep company records and report certain information
- prepare your annual accounts
- complete your Company Tax Return
- file your accounts and your Company Tax Return
- tell other shareholders if you might personally benefit from a transaction the company makes
- pay Corporation Tax

You can hire other people to manage some of these things day-to-day (for example, an accountant) but you’re still legally responsible for your company’s records, accounts and performance.

You may be fined, prosecuted or disqualified from being a company director if you do not meet your responsibilities.

Contact your professional adviser or trade association to find out more.
