# Object to a limited company being struck off

Skip contents

# When you can object

You can object to a limited company being struck off the Companies Register if:

- you are a shareholder or other interested party, such as a creditor
- you have a reason to stop the company being removed from the register - for example, you have a legal claim against them or they owe you money

You can only object after notice that the company is going to be struck off has been published in The Gazette.

You must have evidence to support your objection - for example, invoices or other evidence showing the company owes you money.

You can withdraw your own company’s application to be struck off if you’re a director.

## If the company has already been struck off

If the company has already been struck off, you’ll need to apply for a court order to restore a company instead. You can only do this in certain circumstances - for example, if they owed you money when they were dissolved.

# Overview

You can close down your limited company by getting it ‘struck off’ the Companies Register. This is also known as ‘dissolving’ your company.

You can only strike off your company if it:

- has not traded or sold off any stock in the last 3 months
- has not changed names in the last 3 months
- is not threatened with liquidation
- has no agreements with creditors, for example a Company Voluntary Arrangement (CVA)

If your company does not meet these conditions, you’ll have to voluntarily liquidate your company instead.

When you apply to strike off your company, you have certain responsibilities to close down your business properly.

## After your company is struck off

You’ll lose access to company bank accounts. You will not be able to send or receive money. You’ll have to restore the company to get your bank accounts back.

highlights:
Closing a limited company - GOV.UK

Skip to main content

# Closing a limited company

You usually need to have the agreement of your company’s directors and shareholders to close a limited company.

The way you close the company depends on whether it can pay its bills or not.

## The company can pay its bills (‘solvent’)

You can either:

- apply to get the company struck off the Companies Register
- start a members’ voluntary liquidation

Striking off the company is usually the cheapest way to close it.

## The company cannot pay its bills (‘insolvent’)

When your company is insolvent, the interests of the people your company owes money to (its ‘creditors’) legally come before those of the directors or shareholders.

How you close your company depends on your circumstances. You can:

put your company into administration

apply to get your company struck off the Companies Register

arrange creditors’ voluntary liquidation

You can get professional advice from a solicitor or insolvency practitioner if you’re not sure which option is suitable for your company.

### Compulsory liquidation

Your company might be forced into compulsory liquidation if you do not pay creditors.

You may be able to avoid liquidation by applying for a Company Voluntary Arrangement.

## If the company does not have a director

You must appoint a new director if your company does not have one, for example if a sole director has died.

Companies House will eventually strike off a company that does not have a director but this can make it more difficult to manage any company assets.

Shareholders must agree to appoint a new director and may need to vote on it.

If a sole director has died and there are no shareholders, the executor of the estate can appoint a new director if the company’s articles allow it.

The new director can close the company.

Your company still needs to pay corporation tax and file a tax return even if there’s no director.

## Let the company become dormant

You do not have to close your company if it’s no longer trading. You can let it become ‘dormant’ for tax as long as it’s not:

- carrying on business activity
- trading
- receiving income

Your company will still be registered at Companies House.

You must still send your annual accounts and confirmation statement to Companies House.

You can keep a limited company dormant for as long as you want.

# Liquidate your limited company

Skip contents

# Overview

You can choose to liquidate your limited company (also called ‘winding up’ a company).

There’s a different process if you want to liquidate your limited company in Scotland or wind up your company in Northern Ireland.

The company will stop doing business and employing people. The company will not exist once it’s been removed (‘struck off’) from the companies register at Companies House.

When you liquidate a company, its assets are used to pay off its debts. Any money left goes to shareholders. You’ll need a validation order to access your company bank account.

If that money has not been shared between the shareholders by the time the company is removed from the register, it will go to the state.

You’ll need to restore your company to claim back money after it’s been removed from the register.

There are 3 types of liquidation:

- creditors’ voluntary liquidation- your company cannot pay its debts and you involve your creditors when you liquidate it
- compulsory liquidation- your company cannot pay its debts and you apply to the courts to liquidate it
- members’ voluntary liquidation- your company can pay its debts but you want to close it

Your company may be forced into liquidation if it cannot pay its debts.

Summary:

- The page explains how to apply to have the exact boundary between your property and a neighbour’s recorded by HM Land Registry when your property is registered. This is called a “determined boundary.”
- Who can apply: only if your property is registered. A determined boundary remains valid if either property is sold.
- Before applying: check your title plan/register to see if a determined boundary already exists.
- What you must provide: 
  - Evidence supporting the application
  - A completed exact line of boundary (DB) form
  - A plan showing the determined boundary (preferably prepared by a chartered land surveyor)
  - Supporting documents such as certified pre-registration deeds, expert reports, or written statements witnessed by a solicitor, magistrate, or commissioner of oaths
- Costs: application fee is £90, plus surveyor and solicitor fees.
- Neighbour agreement: if the neighbour agrees, they must sign the form and the plan.
- What happens after a successful application: HM Land Registry updates the title plans/registers for both properties and notifies the neighbour.
- If the neighbour objects: HM Land Registry will assess the objection. If unresolved, the case may go to a tribunal.
  - Tribunal outcome: can either approve a determined boundary (and update registers) or reject/not decide the boundary. You may be responsible for some costs.
- Practical note: consider seeking legal advice before applying, especially if disputes risk escalating to a tribunal.

# Resolving neighbour disputes

Skip contents

# Complain about noise to the council

You can ask your local council for help if the neighbour dispute involves an activity that is damaging to health or a nuisance. This is known as a‘statutory nuisance’.

This could include:

- noise (including loud music and barking dogs)
- artificial light (except street lamps)
- dust, steam, smell or insects from business premises
- smoke, fumes or gases
- a build-up of rubbish that could harm health

Your council has a duty to investigate any statutory nuisance.

You should always try and solve the problem by talking to your neighbour or through mediation before contacting the council.

## Penalties

If the council decides someone is causing a statutory noise nuisance they must issue a ‘noise abatement’ order. This tells the person what they must do to stop making a noise nuisance or else face further legal action.

If someone breaks an abatement order about noise from their home, they can be fined up to £5,000. If it’s noise from a factory or business, the penalty can be up to £20,000.

Skip to main content

# Parental rights and responsibilities

Skip contents

# Who has parental responsibility

You automatically have parental responsibility if you give birth to the child (known as the birth mother).

If you’re a father or second female parent, you might have automatic parental responsibility depending on your circumstances.

## If you have married or formed a civil partnership with the birth mother

You’ll usually have automatic parental responsibility if you’re married to or in a civil partnership with the birth mother when the child is born.

The child’s biological father will automatically get parental responsibility if they marry or enter a civil partnership with the child’s birth mother after the child is born.

### If your child is conceived through fertility treatment

You’ll have automatic parental responsibility if both:

- you’ve married or formed a civil partnership with the birth mother
- you consented to the treatment taking place

## If you have not married or formed a civil partnership with the birth mother

If you have not married or formed a civil partnership with the birth mother, you can get parental responsibility for your child by jointly registering the birth with the mother.

There are different rules for registering a birth for same-sex couples.

If you do not register the birth together, you can apply for parental responsibility.

### If your child is conceived through fertility treatment

You and the birth mother might also need to sign a consent form at a UK licensed fertility clinic if you’ve used donated sperm.

## If a child is born through surrogacy

If a child is born through surrogacy, the surrogate mother who gives birth to the child will have parental responsibility. You can apply for legal parenthood to be transferred.

## Step parents

Step parents do not automatically get parental responsibility for children, even if they’re married to a child’s parent. You can apply for parental responsibility.

- Automatic PR: If you’re the birth mother, you have PR by default. Fathers or second female parents may have automatic PR if they are married/in a civil partnership with the birth mother at birth, or if the parents marry/enter a civil partnership after birth (and in some fertility cases, consent to treatment is required). Same-sex couples have specific registration rules.

Skip to main content

# Parental rights and responsibilities

Skip contents

# What parental responsibility is

Having parental responsibility means you have legal rights and duties relating to your children’s upbringing.

If you have parental responsibility, your most important roles are to:

provide a home for the child

protect and maintain the child

You’re also responsible for:

disciplining the child

choosing and providing for the child’s education

agreeing to the child’s medical treatment

naming the child and agreeing to any change of name

looking after the child’s property

You have to ensure that your child is supported financially, whether you have parental responsibility or not.

There are different rules for parental responsibility in Scotland.

## Parental responsibility for separated parents

If you have parental responsibility for a child but you do not live with them, it does not mean you have a right to spend time with your children. However, the other parent must include you when making important decisions about their lives.

You do not always need to get the consent of the other parent for routine decisions, even if they also have parental responsibility.

If it’s a major decision (for example, one of you wants to move abroad with your children) everyone who has parental responsibility must agree in writing.

You can apply for a Specific Issue Order or Prohibited Steps Order if you cannot agree. A judge will then make a decision which is in your children’s best interests.

You can get help to arrange contact with your children.

# Separating or divorcing: what you need to do

There are certain things you need to do when you separate from your partner in England or Wales.

What you do is different in Scotland and Northern Ireland.

## If you have children

You and your ex-partner must share financial support for your children(‘child maintenance’).

You also need to make arrangements for looking after your children.

Agreeing these things is separate from doing legal paperwork to officially end your relationship.

## Dividing money and property

You have different financial rights, depending on whether you’re separating from:

- your spouse or civil partner
- a partner you’re not married to or in a civil partnership with

### If you’re married or in a civil partnership

You need to agree on how to separate your finances. You must apply to a court for an agreement about your money and property if you want this to be legally binding.

Find out how to:

- get a divorce to officially end your marriage
- officially end your civil partnership

If you do not want to divorce or end your civil partnership you can:

- get a legal separation so you can divide your money and property without ending the relationship officially
- get an annulment if it counts as ‘voidable’ or was never legally valid (‘void’)

### If you’re not married or in a civil partnership

Dividing money and property is different if you’re not married or in a civil partnership.

You do not have the same rights or legal status as married or civil partners, even if you’ve lived together for a long time or have children. ‘Common law marriages’ do not exist in England and Wales.

## Get help or advice

You can get advice about legal paperwork and making arrangements from:

Find a legal adviser if you need legal advice.

Get support and advice from Relate.

# Financial Remedies Court

Administered by HM Courts & Tribunals Service

## What we do

## What is the Financial Remedies Court (FRC)

The FRC is a specialist part of the Family Court. Following the breakdown of a marriage or civil partnership there are often financial issues that need to be resolved.

Financial support for children sometimes falls outside the remit of the Child Maintenance Service. The purpose of the FRC is to ensure that family finances are resolved efficiently by specialist judges.

## How the Financial Remedies Court works

- we operate nationally within the Family Court

- family finance disputes are issued and referred locally to a judge who will assign cases to an allocated judge who is responsible for the progress of that case through the court process
- the Financial Remedies Court has its own protocols and guidelines designed to ensure that cases run smoothly and at all times are overseen by judges who are experienced in this type of work and are nominated by leadership judges to undertake financial work

The GOV.UK page explains how money and property are handled when you and your partner divorce or separate and you want to reach an agreement with your former partner.

Key points:
- It’s generally easier and cheaper to agree on how to divide money and property.

- Typically no court hearing; a judge approves if the proposed order is fair. If not, you may be asked to adjust it.

pages.title: School attendance and absence: Overview - GOV.UK
highlights:
School attendance and absence: Overview - GOV.UK

Skip to main content

# School attendance and absence

Skip contents

# Overview

You must make sure your child gets a full-time education that meets their needs (for example if they have special educational needs).

The guidance is different if you live in Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland.

You can send your child to school or educate them yourself.

Children must get an education between the school term after their 5th birthday and the last Friday in June in the school year they turn 16.

You’ll be contacted by either:

- the school - if your child is enrolled in school and does not turn up (even if they’re only absent for a day)
- the council’s education welfare officer - if they think your child is not getting a suitable education at home

You can be prosecuted if you do not give your child an education. You’ll normally get warnings and offers of help from the local council first.

You can get education and attendance information from your council.

## When your child can miss school

You can only allow your child to miss school if either:

- they’re too ill to go in
- you have advance permission from the school

There’s extra support available if your child cannot go to school for long periods because of a health problem.

There may be other exceptional circumstances where you can ask to take your child out of school. Your school will consider each application and may let you take your child out of school.

### Holidays in term time

A holiday is generally not considered an exceptional circumstance. You cannot usually take your child away during term time.

You can be fined or face legal action for taking your child on holiday during term time.

## School trips

Your child’s school can ask you for a voluntary contribution towards the cost of activities like school trips. They cannot stop your child from attending if you do not pay, but they should cancel the activity if there is not enough money to cover the cost of it.

# Help with getting your child to go to school

If you’re having trouble getting your child to go to school, the school and local council can help.

The school will discuss attendance problems with you and should agree a plan with you to improve your child’s attendance.

A lot of local councils have teams that help parents improve their child’s attendance at school. The council will tell you if they’re able to help. Forms of help could include:

- support to reduce the burden on children where families are in difficulty (for example if a child is spending a lot of time caring for someone)
- working with families and schools to overcome bullying and other serious problems
- a parenting contract

## Parenting contract

This is a voluntary written agreement between you and either the local council or the school’s governing body. Between you, you agree to find ways to improve your child’s attendance.

If you refuse to make a contract or you do not stick to it, it can be used as evidence if the local council decides to prosecute you.

pages.summary:
Summary:

- This section (Education and Inspections Act 2006, s103) creates a duty for parents of a pupil of compulsory school age who is excluded on disciplinary grounds (from a relevant school in England) to keep the pupil out of public places during school hours on days of the exclusion.
- Key requirements:
  - Applies when an exclusion notice under section 104 is given to the parent.
  - On the first five school days of a substantive exclusion (or all days of a short fixed-period exclusion up to five days), the parent must ensure the pupil is not present in a public place during school hours on those days, if stated in the notice.
  - If the pupil is in a public place during school hours on such a day, the parent commits an offence, unless they have a reasonable justification.
  - Offence details: summary conviction, up to a level 3 fine on the standard scale; proceedings can only be brought by the local education authority.
  - If the exclusion occurs part-way through a school day, the remainder of that day counts as a first day for the purposes of the duty.
- Definitions:
  - “Parent” means an individual parent (not non-individual guardians).
  - “Public place” includes highways and any place accessible to the public, with or without payment or permission.
  - “School hours” covers the whole school day session and any breaks within that day.

Practical takeaway for parents:
- If your child is excluded, you must ensure they stay out of public places during school hours on the specified days (up to five days for a standard exclusion), as stated in the exclusion notice. Failure to comply can lead to a fine unless you have a reasonable justification. Local education authorities are responsible for initiating proceedings. For precise obligations, refer to the exclusion notice (section 104) and the exact wording of “public place” and “school hours” in the Act.

Summary:

- The UK Office of the Independent Adjudicator for Higher Education (OIAHE) Rule 7 covers how higher education providers should handle internal processes (complaints, appeals, disciplinary matters, fitness to study/practice, and codes of conduct/regulations).
- Key points:
  - Students are normally expected to pursue internal procedures to completion before contacting the OIAHE, to allow providers to investigate and rectify issues.
  - Internal procedures include: student complaints, academic appeals, disciplinary actions (academic and non-academic), fitness to practise/study, and breaches of codes/regulations.
  - At the end of internal procedures, providers should issue a Completion of Procedures Letter if no further internal avenue exists. The OIAHE has guidance on when such letters are required.
  - In some cases, providers may issue a Completion of Procedures Letter even if the student has not completed all internal stages (e.g., if the student has been signposted but fails to escalate). The OIAHE focuses on whether the provider followed its own procedures.
  - If students raise issues in the Complaint Form that aren’t addressed in the Completion of Procedures Letter, the OIAHE will check which issues were raised internally and decide whether to review them. If a student wants to complain about how the provider handled a complaint or delays, they do not usually need to complete another internal procedure before approaching the OIAHE.
- Practical implication for students in England: follow the provider’s internal processes first; request a Completion of Procedures Letter when appropriate; the OIAHE will assess whether procedures were properly followed, including delays or mishandling of a complaint.

If you’re specifically dealing with an England university complaint and want to know when to contact the OIAHE (as a last resort) or how Completion of Procedures Letters are issued, this page explains the expectations and boundaries of Rule 7. pages.title: Get permission to take a child abroad
highlights:
Get permission to take a child abroad - GOV.UK

Skip to main content

# Get permission to take a child abroad

You must get the permission of everyone with parental responsibility for a child or from a court before taking the child abroad.

Taking a child abroad without permission is child abduction.

You automatically have parental responsibility if you’re the child’s mother, but you still need the permission of anyone else with parental responsibility before you take the child abroad.

You can take a child abroad for 28 days without getting permission if a child arrangement order says the child must live with you, unless a court order says you cannot.

## Get permission from someone with parental responsibility

A letter from the person with parental responsibility for the child is usually enough to show you’ve got permission to take them abroad.

You might be asked for the letter at a UK or foreign border, or if there’s a dispute about taking a child abroad. The letter should include the other person’s contact details and details about the trip.

It also helps if you’ve:

- evidence of your relationship with the child, for example a birth or adoption certificate
- a divorce or marriage certificate, if you are a single parent but your family name is different from the child’s

## Get permission from a court

You’ll need to apply to a court for permission to take a child abroad if you have not got permission from the other people with parental responsibility.

You must give details of the trip, for example the date of departure, when and how you’re returning, and contact details of people with parental responsibility staying in the UK.

You must give more information if you’re taking the child abroad for a longer trip, for example what education the child will get while they’re abroad.

Find a solicitor to get legal advice about permission to take a child abroad.

## Check the age limit in the country you’re travelling to

You need to contact the embassy or consular office of the country you are travelling to for information about the age limit up to which a person is considered a child.

Summary:

The PRACTICE DIRECTION – PRE-ACTION CONDUCT AND PROTOCOLS (Civil Procedure Rules, GOV.UK) explains how parties should behave before starting civil proceedings. Key points:
- Pre-action protocols set the expected steps for specific claim types and are approved by the Master of the Rolls; current protocols are listed in the direction.
- If a relevant protocol exists, parties must follow it before issuing a claim; if none applies, parties should exchange information and correspondence to achieve the objectives, proportionate to the case.
- Typical pre-action steps (when no protocol applies) include:
  - Claimant: send a concise letter detailing the claim’s basis, facts, remedy sought, and how any amount is calculated.
  - Defendant: respond within a reasonable time (e.g., ~14 days for straightforward cases; up to 3 months for very complex ones) with acceptance or reasons for dispute, any counterclaims, and which facts are disputed.
  - Parties disclose key documents relevant to the issues.
- The Practice Direction covers consequences for false statements in pre-action materials (possible contempt of court).
- It also includes a table of protocol applicability and dates into force for various claim types (e.g., Personal Injury, Clinical Negligence, Defamation, Housing Disrepair, etc.).

Summary:
- The page explains lasting power of attorney (LPA) and enduring power of attorney (EPA) for England.
- An LPA lets you appoint attorneys to look after your affairs for the long term and replaces the older EPA system.

# Make, register or end a lasting power of attorney

Skip contents

# Choose your attorney

You can choose one or more people to be your attorney. If you appoint more than one, you must decide whether they’ll make decisions separately or together.

## Who can be your attorney

Your attorney needs to be 18 or over. They could be:

- a relative
- a friend
- a professional, for example a solicitor
- your husband, wife or partner

You must appoint someone who has the mental capacity to make their own decisions.

Your attorney does not need to live in the UK or be a British citizen.

When choosing an attorney, think about:

- how well they look after their own affairs, for example their finances
- how well you know them
- if you trust them to make decisions in your best interests
- how happy they will be to make decisions for you

Read about an attorney’s responsibilities to help you with your decision.

You cannot choose someone who is subject to a Debt Relief Order or someone who is bankrupt if you’re making a lasting power of attorney (LPA) for property and financial affairs.

## If there’s more than one attorney

If you’re appointing more than one person, you must decide if they’ll make decisions:

- separately or together - sometimes called ‘jointly and severally’ - which means attorneys can make decisions on their own or with other attorneys
- together - sometimes called ‘jointly’ - which means all the attorneys have to agree on the decision

You can also choose to let them make some decisions ‘jointly’, and others ‘jointly and severally’.

Attorneys who are appointed jointly must all agree or they cannot make the decision.

## Replacement attorneys

When you make your LPA you can nominate other people to replace your attorney or attorneys if at some point they cannot act on your behalf anymore.

## How to make your own deed poll

You’ll need 2 witnesses to sign your deed poll. They must be 18 or over.

Some organisations will not accept a deed poll if a witness lives at the same address or is a close relative.

Use the following wording. Replace the words in the square brackets with the relevant details.

### Name change deed

“I [old name] of [your address] have given up my name [old name] and have adopted for all purposes the name [new name].

“Where applicable, I have informed the police that I have given up my name [old name] and have adopted the name [new name] and understand that a failure to do so is a criminal offence.

“I also understand that when I apply for official documents in my new name, such as a British Passport, the relevant authorities may check the history and validity of my old name [old name] and new name [new name]. They may also check the information in any other supporting documents they have requested.

“Signed as a deed on [date] as [old name] and [new name] in the presence of [witness 1 name] of [witness 1 address], and [witness 2 name] of [witness 2 address].

“[your new signature], [your old signature]

“[witness 1 signature], [witness 2 signature]”

## After you’ve made your own deed poll

You can use your signed deed poll straight away as proof of your new name.

It’s a criminal offence if you’re a registered offender and you do not tell the police you’ve changed your name.

# Make a subject access request

Due to changes made by the Data (Use and Access) Act, this guidance is under review and may be subject to change. The Plans for new and updated guidance page will tell you about which guidance will be updated and when this will happen.

Use this service to ask an organisation for your personal information or for the information of someone else, eg a child or relative.

This service will create an email to the organisation you specify with your request for personal information and everything they need to respond. You'll also get a copy for your records.

The organisation should reply to you directly. We won't see the reply.

## What you'll need

You will need:

- the name of the organisation you're making your request to; and
- the email address of the organisation. Tip: you can usually find a suitable email address in the organisation's Privacy notice.

You should also provide:

- proof of ID, either a copy of a passport or driving licence; and
- proof of address, either a copy of a bank statement, utility bill, or TV licence.

If you are making the request for someone else, you should provide proof of ID and address for them (not for you). You will also need to provide evidence that you're allowed to make the request for them eg a signed letter of consent, a power of attorney document or proof of parental responsibility such as a birth or adoption certificate.

Start your request for your information

Takes about 10 minutes

For information about what we do with your personal data, see our privacy notice.

# Data protection

# Find out what data an organisation has about you

Write to an organisation to ask for a copy of the information they hold about you.

If it’s a public organisation, write to their Data Protection Officer (DPO). Their details should be on the organisation’s privacy notice.

If the organisation has no DPO, or you do not know who to write to, address your letter to the company secretary.

## How long it should take

The organisation must give you a copy of the data they hold about you as soon as possible, and within 1 month at most.

In certain circumstances, for example particularly complex or multiple requests, the organisation can take a further 2 months to provide data. In this case, they must tell you:

- within 1 month of your request
- why there’s a delay

## When information can be withheld

There are some situations when organisations are allowed to withhold information, for example if the information is about:

- the prevention, detection or investigation of a crime
- national security or the armed forces
- the assessment or collection of tax
- judicial or ministerial appointments

An organisation does not have to say why they’re withholding information.

## How much it costs

Requests for information are usually free. However, organisations can charge an administrative cost in some circumstances, for example if:

- you’re asking for a large amount of information
- your request will take a lot of time and effort to process

# Respond to a data protection request

Under data protection law, anyone can ask if your organisation holds personal information about them - you must respond to their request as soon as possible, and within one month at most.

Requests for personal data should be provided for free in most cases.

Individuals have the right to know:

- what information is being used
- why it’s being used
- where it came from
- who can see the information

## What you must do

You must provide:

- confirmation that you are processing their personal data
- a copy of that data
- details of how that data is collected, used and disposed of

You should send them a hard copy - such as a printout or photocopy. If you received the request by email, you can send the information by email if the requester agrees.

Make sure they can understand the information - for example explain what any codes mean. Your response should be:

- transparent
- written in clear, plain language
- in an easily accessible format

Before you reply you must:

- check the identity of the requester
- remove any data which does not relate to them

You could be fined if you do not respond to the request or provide the information requested.

## Exemptions

You might not need to give all the personal information you have about someone if requested - for example, if it contains legal advice or relates to another person.

## Further information

Find out more about how to respond to requests. For further advice, contact the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO).

‘Right to reside’ means you have the right to live in the UK.

You have a right to reside in the UK if any of the following is true:

- you have ‘right of abode’ in the UK, if you’re a British citizen

You do not have the right to reside but can stay in the UK while you have one of the following:

# How to apply for a visa to come to the UK

Skip contents

# Overview

You may need a visa to come to the UK to study, work, visit or join family.

There are different visas depending on:

- where you come from
- why you want to come to the UK
- how long you want to stay for
- your personal circumstances and skills

You may be able to apply for an electronic travel authorisation (ETA) instead of a visa. This depends on your nationality and your reason for coming to the UK, for example if you’re visiting or transiting through a UK airport.

You do not need to apply for a visa if you’re an Irish citizen.

## What you need to do

Check if you need a visa. The check if you need a visa tool will tell you what your options are.

Prepare any evidence and documents you need for your application.

Apply online. As part of the application process, you’ll be asked to provide any evidence and documents required and pay the fee.

Provide biometrics (fingerprints and photograph).

Get your decision. It usually takes between 3 and 12 weeks to get a decision on your application, so you’ll need to apply with enough time before you travel.

## When to apply

The earliest you can apply for a visa is usually:

- 3 months before your planned travel date for visit visas
- 3 months before your employment start date for most work visas
- 6 months before your course start date for Student and Child Student visas

You can check how long it will take to get a decision online.

## Preparing your evidence

When applying for a visa, you’ll need to:

- usually have a valid passport or travel document
- provide supporting evidence as part of your application
- provide certified translations of any documents that are not in English or Welsh

You may also need to provide additional evidence depending on the visa and your circumstances - for example, a tuberculosis (TB) test result or evidence of your English language ability.

You’re looking for UK guidance on council tax summonses and related debt issues (especially in England) within the Citizens Advice / GOV.UK framework, including interactions with Universal Credit.

Key takeaways from Citizens Advice (England):

Summary:

This page outlines the Pre-Action Protocol for the Resolution of Clinical Disputes under Civil Procedure Rules (UK). It applies to claims against hospitals, GPs, dentists, and other healthcare providers (NHS and private) where injury is alleged to result from clinical negligence, and it excludes claims covered by other specific procedures.

Key points:
- Encourages a transparent, “cards-on-the-table” approach to resolving disputes before court action.
- Requires early notification and collection of facts, records, and expert input when needed; a Letter of Notification may precede a Letter of Claim.
- A Letter of Claim should outline the facts, alleged adverse outcome, and main negligence allegations; copies should be sent to NHS indemnity bodies (e.g., NHSLA) as applicable.
- Do not issue court proceedings until four months after the Letter of Claim (extension possible in some cases); if proceedings begin early, parties should seek a court stay to complete pre-action steps.
- The defendant must provide a reasoned response (Letter of Response) within four months of the Letter of Claim, addressing the claim’s merits and potential extensions of time.
- The protocol supports early steps to resolve disputes without litigation, including consideration of medical reports and expert advice as needed.

If you are looking to complain about NHS clinical negligence in England, this protocol explains the recommended pre-action steps and timelines before pursuing court action, and how information should be exchanged with NHS bodies and indemnifiers. For practical complaint routes, consider NHS England/NHS Improvement guidance, NHS.UK complaint processes, and Citizens Advice resources.

# Buying a home

# Overview

Buying a home takes about 5 months on average. The process can take longer if you’re part of a chain of buyers and sellers.

If you’re also selling a home, read the guide to selling your home.

This guide is for England and Wales. There are different rules for buying a home in Scotland and buying a home in Northern Ireland.

To buy a home, you’ll need to:

- decide how much you need to borrow - you may be able to get financial help from the government through an affordable home ownership scheme
- choose a mortgage lender
- choose a property
- make an offer on a property
- exchange contracts - if the seller accepts your offer, they’re responsible for drawing up a legal contract to transfer ownership
- pay tax
- arrange and pay for searches and surveys
- arrange for a removals company to help you move home

An offer is not legally binding until contracts are exchanged.

You may be able to get financial help from the government through an affordable home ownership scheme.

## If you’re buying property with someone else

You can own a home with up to 3 other people. Find out more about the different types of joint property ownership.

## Protecting yourself from fraud

There’s a risk of fraud when buying a home as this involves transferring large sums of money. It’s important to check that you:

- are speaking to or emailing the person or business you think it is
- transfer money to the correct bank account/s
- do not reveal too much personal information on social media

You can also speak to a legal professional for help and advice about property fraud.

- the other owner has lost mental capacity

- you’re selling for someone else using power of attorney

Check what you need to do to sell a property for someone else.

## Choosing a buyer

Buyers can make offers verbally (over the phone or in person) or in writing.

If you’re using an estate agent to sell your home, buyers must make an offer through them. Your estate agent must inform you of any offers made.

If you’re selling your home privately, buyers can make offers directly to you.

Once you’ve accepted an offer, the buyer’s solicitor or conveyancer will arrange searches and a review of the property’s title.

# Controlling your dog in public

Skip contents

# Overview

It’s against the law to let a dog be dangerously out of control anywhere, such as:

- in a public place
- in a private place, for example a neighbour’s house or garden
- in the owner’s home

The law applies to all dogs.

You can report a dog that’s out of control.

Some types of dogs are banned.

XL Bully dogs are now banned in England and Wales. Check what to do if you own an XL Bully dog.

## Out of control

Your dog is considered dangerously out of control if it:

- injures someone
- makes someone worried that it might injure them

A court could also decide that your dog is dangerously out of control if either of the following apply:

- it attacks someone’s animal
- the owner of an animal thinks they could be injured if they tried to stop your dog attacking their animal

## Penalties

You can get an unlimited fine or be sent to prison for up to 6 months (or both) if your dog is dangerously out of control. You may not be allowed to own a dog in the future and your dog may be destroyed.

If you let your dog injure someone you can be sent to prison for up to 5 years or fined (or both). If you deliberately use your dog to injure someone you could be charged with ‘malicious wounding’.

If you allow your dog to kill someone you can be sent to prison for up to 14 years or get an unlimited fine (or both).

If you allow your dog to injure an assistance dog (for example a guide dog) you can be sent to prison for up to 3 years or fined (or both).

pages.summary:
Summary:

The GOV.UK guidance on "Control dogs" explains the powers available to police, councils and other authorities in England to control or improve a dog’s behaviour, including when a dog is dangerous, banned, or causing nuisance. Key mechanisms include:

- Community Protection Notice (CPN): requires the person responsible for the dog to stop or control its behaviour if it’s persistent, unreasonable and affects quality of life.
- Civil injunction: targets antisocial or harmful dog behaviour; can be issued to someone aged 10+ and may include restrictions (eg, areas, on-lead requirements) after court approval based on balance of probability.
- Public Spaces Protection Order (PSPO): councils can restrict dog activities in public spaces (parks, town centres) where behaviour meets specified conditions.
- Criminal Behaviour Order (CBO): for individuals (16+) with certain dog-related behaviours that cause harassment, alarm or distress.
- DLO (Dog Legislation Officer): every police service should have a trained officer or accessible procedures to obtain one.

Application scope: Applies to England. The page outlines when authorities can act to prevent harm, nuisance, or antisocial behaviour caused by dogs, with emphasis on reasonable measures and appropriate tailoring to the severity and frequency of the behaviour.

If you’re seeking guidance for a neighbor dispute or suspected animal cruelty, this page details official enforcement options and the process (CPN, injunctions, PSPOs) available to authorities, rather than reporting processes for non-government bodies (such as the RSPCA). For reporting animal cruelty, you’d typically contact the RSPCA or local authority’s animal welfare team.

This CPS guidance explains prosecutions under the Dangerous Dogs Act 1991 for dogs that are “dangerously out of control.” Key points:

- Offence: Under section 3, if a dog is dangerously out of control in any place (including private property), the owner or person in charge commits a summary offence. Prosecution must show that the defendant’s act or omission caused or permitted the dog to be dangerously out of control to more than a minimal degree; recklessness or intent need not be proven. No defence that the owner did not expect the dog to behave that way (Bezzina principle).
- Aggravated offence: The offence becomes aggravated (triable either way) if the dog injures a person or an assistance dog while out of control.
- Threshold of “dangerously out of control”: There is consideration that a dog injuring or threatening to injure a person or assistance dog, or chasing livestock or harming livestock, can demonstrate dangerousness, with reference to related livestock Acts for civil liability and definitions of cattle and poultry.
- Lawful purpose: Guidance references decisions (e.g., R v PY) on when a dog is considered to be acting under a lawful purpose for Crown or constable purposes.
- Animal welfare links: The guidance notes that injuries to animals may be relevant to assessing danger but do not automatically prove the offence; a careful, statutory test and ordinary meaning apply.
- Scope: The guidance covers prohibited dogs and general dangerousness, including evidential and public interest considerations and charge selection.

Summary tailored to your query (England-focused; official guidance and enforcement)

- What it is: The Animal Welfare Act 2006 (England) sets out duties of animal ownership and enforcement powers to prevent cruelty, neglect, and harm to animals in England. It covers responsibility for animals, prevention of harm, dealing with distress, and powers to intervene.

- Key provisions relevant to dogs and harm:
  - Section 3: Responsibility for animals — owners must meet welfare standards.
  - Section 4–5: Prevention of harm — duties to ensure welfare (adequate food, water, shelter, manner of care).
  - Section 6: Docking of dogs’ tails — restrictions and bans on routine tail docking.
  - Section 8: Fighting etc. — offences related to involvement with animal fighting.
  - Sections on animals in distress (including duties and powers to intervene) and seizure powers (e.g., in distress or fighting scenarios).

# Caring for pets

You must provide proper care to any animal you keep as a pet.

You may get an unlimited fine or be sent to prison for up to 6 months if you do not look after an animal properly. You may also be banned from owning animals in future.

## How to care for your pet

You must make sure that any animal you own or care for:

- has a proper diet and fresh water
- has somewhere suitable to live
- is kept with or away from other animals, depending on its needs
- is allowed to express itself and behave normally
- is protected from, and treated for, illness and injury

You must be over 16 years old to buy an animal.

## Microchipping your pet

You must make sure your dog is microchipped.

The rules for cats depend on where you live.

Check the rules about microchipping dogs and cats.

## Licences

You do not need a licence to own or keep most common pets, such as cats or dogs.

You may need a licence from your local council if you:

- keep wild or exotic animals
- run a business that involves pets, such as breeding, boarding or selling them

Find out about activities that need a pet licence.

Contact your local council to apply for a licence or to check if you need one. You must get the licence before you get the animal.

## Report cruelty to animals

### England or Wales

Contact the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (RSPCA) to report someone neglecting or being cruel to an animal in England or Wales.

RSPCA cruelty and advice line 0300 1234 999 8am to 6pm Find out about call charges

You can also report concerns online.

### Scotland

Contact the Scottish Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (SSPCA):

SSPCA animal helpline 03000 999 999 7am to 11pm Find out about call charges

You’ll be asked to give a detailed description of what you’ve seen or heard. You do not have to give your personal details if you do not want to.

# Defend your intellectual property

Skip contents

# Take legal action

You can file legal proceedings either through the Intellectual Property Office (IPO) or through the courts.

Some types of proceedings can only be filed through one or the other. For example, copyright infringement claims can only be filed through the courts.

A court will expect you to have tried to resolve your dispute - possibly using mediation- before starting legal proceedings.

You can pay an Intellectual Property Professional to help you.

## File through IPO

Contact IPO for more information on filing through them.

## File through the courts in England and Wales

The court you go to depends on the nature, complexity and value of your claim.

### Claims below £10,000

Use the Intellectual Property Enterprise Court (IPEC) small claims track if your claim is for less than £10,000 and for infringement of one of the following:

- copyright
- passing off
- trade marks
- breach of confidence
- unregistered design rights

You do not need a lawyer to use the IPEC small claims track.

### Claims up to £500,000

You can take a case for any IP right to the Intellectual Property Enterprise Court (IPEC) if you do not wish to claim more than:

- £60,000 for legal costs
- £500,000 for damages

### If you’re claiming more than £500,000 in damages

Use the Chancery Division of the High Court of England and Wales- there are no limits to legal costs or damages you can claim.

## File through the courts in Scotland

Use the Court of Session if your claim is complex or valuable - there are no limits to legal costs or damages you can claim.

## File through the courts in Northern Ireland

You can use the Chancery Division of the High Court of Northern Ireland if your claim is complex or valuable - there are no limits to legal costs or damages you can claim.

Skip to main content

Guidance

# Enforcing your copyright

How to enforce copyright when somebody uses your work without your permission.

From: Intellectual Property Office Published 29 May 2014 Last updated 23 February 2016 — See all updates

Get emails about this page

Print this page

## Overview

Copyright is a private right. Decisions about how to enforce your right, ie what to do when someone uses your copyright work without your permission, are for you to take.

Infringement is where someone uses the whole or a substantial part of your work without your permission and none of the exceptions to copyright apply.

IP BASICS: Someone is using my IP

Although you do not have to, it will usually be sensible, and save you time and money, to try to resolve the matter with the party you think has infringed your copyright. In some cases it may be necessary to show the court that you have tried to solve the matter with the other party. Mediation is one way of resolving an issue before starting court proceedings.

If you cannot resolve the matter with the other party, then going to court may be the right solution. But it would be a good idea to seek legal advice at an early stage, and to consider alternative solutions such as mediation before going to court.

One of the many organisations representing copyright owners may also be able to give you advice, or, if you are a member, sometimes act on your behalf.

If you do go to court, the courts can:

- stop that person making further infringing use of the material by granting an injunction
- award the copyright owner damages
- make the infringing party give up the goods to the copyright owner

Deliberate infringement of copyright on a commercial scale may be a criminal offence .

## Substantial part

A substantial part is not defined in copyright law but has been interpreted by the courts to mean a qualitatively significant part of a work even where this is not a large part of the work. Therefore, it is quite likely that even a small portion of the whole work will still be a substantial part.

# Trade marks

To use an existing trade mark you should contact the current owner.

Find the owner of a registered trade mark by searching the trade marks database.

## Licensing

A licence is a formal agreement to use someone else’s trade mark. You and the owner must agree the terms of the licence, for example the cost or how long it will last.

When you’ve agreed a licence to use the trade mark, fill in the form to record a licensee and post it. The address is on the form.

Post an application to remove or amend the record of a licence when the licensing agreement ends or if you need to change it.

The owner must sign any form you send, or you must send proof of the agreement with your application.

Each application costs £60.

## Buying

You must tell IPO if you become the new owner of a trade mark, for example by buying it or as the result of a company merger.

In some cases the owner may only sell you one part of a trade mark, for example they may not sell the right to register derivative marks. This is known as a ‘partial assignment’.

Use either:

- ‘Application to record a change of ownership’ form
- ‘Application to record a partial assignment of goods and/or services’ form

Each application costs £60.

Fill in the form and post it. The address is on the form.

## Coexistence agreements

You may be able to use an identical trade mark (for example company name, logo) as someone else by making a coexistence agreement.

This means you agree that both of you can continue to use the trade mark.

# Overview

It’s your responsibility to defend your intellectual property (IP) and to take action if someone’s used it without permission (known as ‘infringement’).

Examples of IP infringement include when someone:

- uses, sells or imports your patented product or process
- uses all or some of your work under copyright without your permission
- makes, offers or sells your registered design for commercial gain
- uses a trade mark that’s identical or similar to one you’ve registered

You can take the following steps.

Get the other party to stop using your IP or come to an agreement with them, for example license your IP.

Use mediation or another type of dispute resolution.

Take legal action if you cannot resolve the dispute by other means.

You may want to get help from an IP professional, such as a solicitor. The Intellectual Property Office (IPO) can also help.

## Report IP crime

It can be a criminal offence to copy or use copyright material and registered trade marks and designs without permission.

Report suspected IP crime to Trading Standards by contacting Citizens Advice.

Summary:

- The content excerpt is from the UK Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 (section on criticism, review, and news reporting), focusing on fair dealing and quotations.
- Key points:
  - Fair dealing for criticism or review of a work (or another work or a performance) is not copyright infringement if:
    - accompanied by a sufficient acknowledgement (unless impracticable),
    - the work has been made available to the public.
  - A quoted passage can be used if:
    - the work has been made public,
    - the use is fair dealing,
    - the quotation is no longer than necessary for the purpose,
    - sufficient acknowledgement is provided (unless impracticable).
  - “Made available to the public” includes various means such as public copies, electronic access, lending, public performance/exhibition, or communication to the public; unauthorised acts don’t count when determining availability.
  - For reporting current events, fair dealing is allowed for works (except photographs) if accompanied by sufficient acknowledgement, with some exceptions where acknowledgement is impractical (sound recordings/films/broadcasts).

How this relates to your query (England using copyrighted material in a music video, fair dealing, IPO, UK guidance):
- Fair dealing defenses exist for criticism, review, or reporting current events, but there is no general “free use” for music videos.
- Using copyrighted music in a video in the UK could infringe unless you can fit a fair dealing exception:
  - It would need to be clearly for criticism/review of the work or for reporting current events, with proper and sufficient acknowledgement, and the usage must be no more than necessary for the purpose.
  - The defense applies to most works but is stricter for recordings, broadcasts, and certain other formats; substantial permission (license) is typically required for music videos.
- For official guidance, see UK GOV.UK and Citizens Advice resources on copyright, fair dealing, and licensing, as well as guidance from IPO (Intellectual Property Office) on fair dealing and licensing for music/video uses.

# Find out if you need a licence to copy a creative work

You must ask the owner if you want to copy a ‘creative work’, for example:

- a diary
- a photograph
- a film
- music

If you do not know who the owner is you might need an ‘orphan works licence’ to copy the work. You should:

See if the work is covered by copyright- if it’s not, you do not need a licence to copy it.

Read the copyright exceptions- if the work is covered by an exception, you do not need a licence to copy it.

Do a diligent search to see if you can find out who owns the work you want to copy - read the guidance on how to do a diligent search depending on whether it’s a literary, still visual art or film and sound work.

Apply for a licence if the work is not covered by an exception or you cannot find the owner - read the orphan works licence guidance to find out how to apply for a licence.

...
# Am I entitled to compensation?
...
If a flight you’re booked on is delayed or cancelled, you may be entitled to compensation – but only when the airline is at fault.
...
Under UK law, airlines are required to pay compensation to passengers when their flights are delayed or cancelled. However, you only have the right to compensation in some circumstances.
...
There are two key factors:
...
- How severely you have been inconvenienced. For instance, if you have only been delayed slightly, you may not be entitled to compensation.
- The cause of the delay. If the delay was caused by an 'extraordinary circumstance' you will not be entitled to compensation.
...
UK law on flight compensation uses the term 'extraordinary circumstances' to refer to situations where delays or cancellations have been caused by things that are not the responsibility of the airline. If extraordinary circumstances apply, you are not entitled to compensation.
...
The Regulation does not define “extraordinary circumstances” and there have been a number of cases in the European (before the UK left the EU) and English courts regarding what the term covers. The cases have centred on whether technical faults on an aircraft could be an extraordinary circumstance. In June 2014 the English Court of Appeal issued a judgment in the Jet2 v Huzar case which provided clarity in the UK that technical problems were not an extraordinary circumstance.
...
If you are not sure whether extraordinary circumstances apply to your flight, but have read about your other rights and think you might have a case, you can make a claim to your airline for compensation. The airline should explain to you the reason for the disruption. If they consider it was due to extraordinary circumstances they will need to clearly set out why. If they reject your claim then you can consider whether to pursue it further.
...
## How to claim
...
If you think you have a strong case for compensation, see how to lodge a claim with your airline.

- When you pay, you should receive an ATOL Certificate with the ATOL holder’s name and number, protecting your payment if the agent stops trading. If you don’t receive it, ask for one and contact the CAA for advice.
- If you have an ATOL Certificate, contact the named ATOL holder first. If there’s no ATOL reference but an airline is known, check with the airline about your booking details.
- If issues arise, you risk losing payments and flights. Check with the airline to see if your booking exists under an ATOL booking. Retail agents typically don’t deal directly with airlines; ATOL holders do.
- If the agent is in a trade association, contact that association for advice. Also contact ATOL Enforcement.
- Package Holidays rights are governed by the Package Travel Regulations 1992 (Regulations 11–13 cover changes before departure; Regulations 14–15 cover problems in resort; enforced by Local Trading Standards).
- If the agent is a member of a trade association, contact them first. If you have an ATOL Certificate, verify the booking status with the ATOL holder named on it and use the online ATOL holders database for contact details.
- Check with the airline to confirm whether they have your booking and its status. If the agent is not part of a trade association and has not booked you with an ATOL holder, your payments may be at risk.
- For additional consumer help, you can contact Citizens Advice.

Relevance to your query: The page provides official guidance on England-specific ATOL protections, how to pursue compensation or refunds when dealing with travel agents, and where to seek help (ATOL, airline, trade associations, Trading Standards, Citizens Advice). It directly addresses ATOL claims, airline contact points, and consumer rights under the Package Travel Regulations. If you’re specifically seeking UK official guidance on England package holidays, ATOL claims, and Citizens Advice resources, this page is authoritative.

# Using CCTV

If your business uses CCTV, you must register your details with the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) and pay a data protection fee, unless you are exempt.

Check if you need to pay the data protection fee.

You must also:

- tell people they may be recorded, usually by displaying signs, which must be clearly visible and readable
- control who can see the recordings
- make sure the system is only used for the purpose it was intended for - for example, if it was set up to detect crime, you must not use it to monitor how much work your staff do

The ICO has guidance with more details about CCTV.

## How to pay the fee

You can register and pay the fee online.

## Letting people see CCTV recordings

Anyone can ask to see images that you’ve recorded of them. Usually, you must usually provide the footage free of charge within 1 calendar month.

Find out more about CCTV and data protection rules.

Data protection rules do not apply if you install a camera on your own home for household purposes - for example, to protect it from burglary. Find out more about using CCTV in the home.

Summary:
The ICO guidance on paying the data protection fee applies to the “households sector” and outlines when an organisation must pay for processing personal data, including CCTV activities. Key points:
- CCTV on business premises for crime prevention generally requires payment if the purpose is not solely for personal/household use.
- If an entity is a limited company for communal area maintenance (property management), this is not exempt and a fee may be due for processing personal data (resident information, financials, maintenance, supplier decisions, CCTV, dispute resolution, etc.).
- If you are processing only personal, family, or household information (not business-related), you may be exempt from paying.
- Exempt examples include purely personal activities (e.g., a dashcam used strictly for work on a vehicle may still require a fee if used for work; personal use in the household with no commercial activity is typically exempt).
- Images from CCTV are personal data; if crime prevention is not the business purpose, you still may need to pay.
- The guidance also notes that individuals acting in purely personal, family, or household capacities are exempt.

If you’re looking specifically for guidance relevant to England, domestic CCTV, neighbours, and official UK guidance (Citizens Advice, GOV.UK), this ICO page clarifies when fees apply and clarifies exemptions. pages.summary:
Summary:

- Pre-charge bail: If police arrest someone on reasonable grounds to believe bail conditions were breached, they may arrest for breach under s.46A PACE. A breach of pre-charge bail is not itself a criminal offence, though it can coincide with other offences (e.g., assault, witness intimidation) for which separate charges may be pursued.
- Court handling: There is no formal provision to refer alleged breaches of pre-charge bail to the court in the same way as post-charge bail.
- Detention decisions: After arrest, police decide whether to charge the person with the original offence for which bail was given. If charging authorization is not yet given, it can be sought while detained.
- Threshold Test: A suspected breach may require applying the Threshold Test if it wasn’t previously met.
- Release options: If no charge is authorised, the suspect may be released without charge, either on bail or without bail (s.37C(2)(b) PACE). If released on bail, conditions in place immediately before arrest for the breach remain; conditions cannot be varied.
- Arrest timing with new offences: If the arrest involves a new offence and a breach, police should consider charging both within 24 hours and present the person to a magistrates’ court within 24 hours, even if the new offence investigation isn’t complete. If impracticable, police may delay the arrest under Bail Act provisions and complete enquiries first.

If you’re looking for practical steps after an NFA (no further action) decision, or how bail conditions work in England, this guidance clarifies that:
- Breaches of pre-charge bail are not automatically criminal; they may lead to separate charges if other offences are involved.
- There’s no automatic court referral for bail breaches; decisions focus on charging the initial offence and any new offences.
- Release on bail keeps prior breach conditions unless the police obtain authority to charge or modify conditions through proper channels.

# Being charged with a crime

Skip contents

# Bail

When you’re waiting for a court hearing or a trial, you might be given bail. This means you can be released from custody until the hearing or the trial.

## Bail from a police station

You can be given bail at the police station after you’ve been charged. This means you’ll be released from custody until your first court hearing.

If you’re given bail, you might have to agree to conditions like:

- living at a particular address
- not contacting certain people
- giving your passport to the police so you cannot leave the UK
- reporting to a police station at agreed times, for example once a week

If you do not stick to these conditions you can be arrested again and be taken to prison to wait for your court hearing.

## Bail from a court

When you’ve been charged and you attend your hearing at a magistrates’ court, you might be given bail until your trial begins.

You may not be given bail if:

- you’ve been convicted of a crime in the past
- you’ve been given bail in the past and not stuck to the terms
- the court thinks you might not turn up for your next hearing
- the court thinks you might commit a crime while you’re on bail

If you’re given bail, you might have to agree to conditions like:

- living at a particular address
- not contacting certain people
- giving up your passport so you cannot leave the UK

If you do not stick to these conditions, you can be arrested again. You’ll stay in police custody until you’re given another court hearing.

The court may put different conditions in place for your bail or keep you in prison until your trial starts.

## If you’re under 18

The police will explain the rules that you have to follow and what will happen if you do not. They will also tell you whether you have temporarily become a ‘looked after child’ and what this means.

If you’re not released from custody, your local authority and the Youth Justice Service must try to find a safe and secure space for you (for example, with a relative, in foster care or in a children’s home). You must stay there until the next available court hearing, which is normally the next day.

If you are not moved to a secure space, you will stay at the police station. The police must present a certificate to the court to explain why you’ve been kept there.

Summary:

- Topic: The Criminal Procedure Rules 2025, focusing on defendant applications or appeals to the Crown Court after a magistrates’ court bail decision.
- Key provisions:
  - When the defendant can apply to the Crown Court for bail after magistrates’ court decisions (bail being withheld or a bail condition being refused/varied).
  - Requirements for the application:
    - Submit in writing as soon as practicable after the magistrates’ decision.
    - Include: why the Crown Court should not withhold bail or should vary the condition, any new information or legal argument since the magistrates’ decision, terms of any suggested bail condition, and, if applicable, a reason for an earlier hearing. Attach the certificate of full argument served under rule 14.4(4).
  - Procedural steps:
    - Magistrates’ court officer must promptly serve relevant documents on the Crown Court officer.
    - The Crown Court should hear the application/appeal as soon as practicable, and no later than the business day after service, unless directed otherwise.
  - Legal background and limits:
    - Crown Court bail powers under section 81 of the Senior Courts Act 1981 (bail in cases where magistrates’ court withheld bail).
    - Right to appeal bail conditions to the Crown Court under section 16 of the Criminal Justice Act 2003, limited to specific types of conditions (e.g., residence, surety, curfews, electronic monitoring, no-contact orders) and where the magistrates’ court has for varying those conditions.
  - Extraditions:
    - In extradition cases, the High Court may grant or vary bail conditions on the defendant’s application under section 22 of the Criminal Justice Act 1967, with procedure guided by Civil Procedure Rules Schedule 1 (RSC Order 79).

What this means in practice (relevant to your terms: England, bail, court summons, Crown Court, magistrates, CPS, GOV.UK, Citizens Advice):
- If a magistrates’ court has withheld bail or refused/varied a bail condition, the defendant may apply to the Crown Court for bail or for variation of the condition.
- The application must be written, include arguments and any new information, and propose a bail condition if applicable.
- The process is expedited: the hearing should occur promptly after service to the Crown Court.
- The ability to appeal certain bail conditions to the Crown Court is limited to specific types of conditions listed in the Criminal Justice Act 2003.

Summary:

- This is Part 14 (Bail) of The Criminal Procedure Rules 2025 (UK Statutory Instrument 2025/909).
- Rule 14.14 covers requirements that a court may impose as bail conditions, specifically:
  - (a) a surety
  - (b) a payment
  - (c) the surrender of a document or thing
- The court may specify how these conditions are to be met.
- If a recognizance is required (usually with a surety):
  - The recognizance must set out the amount payable if the condition isn’t fulfilled and the expiry date/event.
  - The surety must enter into the recognizance in the presence of a court officer, the defendant’s custodian (if in custody), or an authorised person.
  - The person before whom the recognizance is entered must immediately serve a copy on the surety (and, where relevant, on the court officer and the defendant’s custodian).
- If a payment or surrender of a document/thing is required:
  - Payment/document/thing must be made or surrendered to the court officer, the defendant’s custodian (if in custody), or an authorised person.
  - The court officer or custodian must promptly inform the other party that the payment/document/thing has been made or surrendered.
- The custodian must release the defendant when all ordered bail requirements are met.
- Note references to section 119 of the Magistrates’ Courts Act 1980.

# Police cautions, warnings and penalty notices

The police or Crown Prosecution Service can give you a caution (warning) or a penalty notice if you commit a minor crime.

The rules are different in Scotland.

## Cautions

Cautions are given to anyone aged 10 or over for minor crimes - for example writing graffiti on a bus shelter.

You have to admit an offence and agree to be cautioned. You can be arrested and charged if you do not agree.

A caution is not a criminal conviction, but it could be used as evidence of bad character if you go to court for another crime.

Cautions can show on standard and enhanced Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS) checks.

## Conditional cautions

You have to stick to certain rules and restrictions as part of a conditional caution, for example:

- going for treatment for drug abuse
- fixing damage to a property

You could be charged with a crime if you do not stick to the conditions.

## Penalty notices for disorder

Penalty notices for disorder are given for offences like:

- shoplifting
- possessing cannabis
- being drunk and disorderly in public

You can only get a penalty notice if you’re 18 or over.

You’ll be asked to sign the penalty notice ticket. You will not get a criminal conviction if you pay the penalty.

You can ask for a trial if you disagree with the penalty notice. You’ll get a bigger fine if you do not ask for a trial but do not pay the fine.

You can pay a fixed penalty online.

Summary:
The document from the CPS (England) explains key steps after police caution or case review decisions:
- No Further Action (NFA): If the CPS decides the case doesn’t pass its two-stage test and no further evidence could change this, they will take no charge. If unhappy, you can request a formal Victim/Complainant Review; start the review soon after notification, ideally within 10 working days (two weeks), and generally within three months unless exceptional circumstances apply.
- Bail: If a defendant is released on bail, they must attend court at each stage but aren’t kept in prison between hearings. If not released on bail, they are held in custody until trial. Bail decisions involve arguments between the CPS prosecutor and defense, with the court or magistrates deciding on bail. Conditions may be imposed (e.g., surrendering a passport, no contact with you, staying away from home area). Breaching conditions can lead to remand in custody. If you suspect a breach or have concerns, contact the police promptly.

14.11 Where a suspect has been arrested under section 46A of PACE, the detention clock is paused for a period of three hours (s 47(6A)). This begins when the suspect arrives at the police station and is still regarded as a PACE detention. This means that when someone is arrested for breach of bail, the suspect can be held for up to three hours without any effect on the original clock. This time is lost once the suspect is released – it is not cumulative and sits aside, or separate, from the original clock. Each instance of breach of bail attracts a separate three-hour pause. For example, a suspect arrested for a second breach cannot have any unused time from the first breach added on.

14.13 When a suspect is arrested for a breach of pre-charge bail, the overriding objective is to progress the investigation to a full code test charging decision. This will not always be possible depending on the circumstances of the case, outstanding investigative actions and the point when the breach has occurred (for example, a few hours, days, weeks or months after release). The three-hour pause can be used with any time remaining on the original detention clock. The pause should not be used punitively.
pages.summary:
Summary:
The GOV.UK guidance on pre-charge bail explains how police handle breaches of pre-charge bail and what happens next. Key points:

- Bail decisions (section 37(7)(a) of PACE) occur when there is enough evidence to charge and only the CPS charging decision remains outstanding.
- If a suspect breaches bail, police should take positive action, including arrest for breach or for a substantive offence, to deter further offending and reassure victims/witnesses.
- When a suspect is arrested for breach, the custody officer decides whether they should be charged or released without charge. Bail conditions cannot be changed or removed without proper process.
- Detention clock rules:
  - For breach arrests under PACE, a three-hour pause to the detention clock applies (under section 46A/47(6A)); this pause starts on arrival at the station and is non-cumulative across breaches.
  - Each breach of bail triggers a separate three-hour pause; unused time from a prior breach cannot be carried forward.
- The overriding objective after a breach of pre-charge bail is to progress toward a full code test charging decision. Depending on case circumstances, achieving this may be delayed by ongoing investigative actions or the timing of the breach.

In short, breaches lead to potential arrest, a custody decision on charging, and explicit detention-clock pauses, all aimed at advancing toward a charging decision while ensuring proportionality and accountability. If you’re seeking precise procedures for a specific scenario (e.g., NFA or CPS action after a breach), consult the sections on arrest, detention clocks, and charging decisions in the GOV.UK pre-charge bail guidance.

## Details

This document provides guidance on the pre-charge bail regime in England and Wales, to be read in conjunction with the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984. The guidance is approved by the Secretary of State for the Home Office, laid in Parliament and published by the College of Policing.

All those who exercise functions relating to pre-charge bail should follow this guidance – with the exception of members of the Serious Fraud Office, Financial Conduct Authority, National Crime Agency or HM Revenue and Customs. These agencies will have their own guidance on their pre-charge bail regimes.

Summary:

The page is a guide to finding legal help in Scotland. It highlights where to get free or affordable advice on common problems such as benefits, housing, and employment, including:

- Citizens Advice Scotland (CAS): free advice by phone or in person; contact at 0800 028 1456 (Mon–Fri, 9am–5pm). Website linked.
- Employment issues: can contact CAS or a trade union; ACAS can help with early dispute resolution; if unresolved, you may pursue an employment tribunal. Legal advice from a solicitor is available, and legal aid may be available if you cannot afford it.
- Housing: Shelter Scotland offers free helpline (0808 800 4444) and court/advocacy support; local councils can offer rent/mortgage advice even if not in council housing; a solicitor can advise on housing matters and representation, with legal aid as an option.
- General legal help: a solicitor can provide advice and representation; legal aid may be available if costs are unaffordable.

If your query concerns Scottish consumer, employment, or housing rights, this page points you to official UK/Scottish sources for free or affordable guidance and steps to pursue tribunals or court action if needed. It references no external links beyond CAS/Shelter guidance and does not cover non-housing consumer issues in detail.

Problems with your employer usually fall into one of two categories:

- grievances – when you raise your concerns, problems or complaints with your employer
- disciplinaries – when your employer has concerns about your work, conduct or absence

Explain your concern to your manager to see if you can sort out any problems informally. You may find it helpful to suggest what you would like them to do to solve your problem.

Your employer should discuss any disciplinary issues with you informally first. These issues could lead to formal disciplinary action, including dismissal in more serious or repetitive cases.
