The nidirect article explains fundamental and situation-specific rights in Northern Ireland, protected by the UK Human Rights Act 1998. Key points include:
- Everyone in Northern Ireland has fundamental human rights that public authorities must respect, with additional rights arising in specific situations (e.g., at work).
- Core rights cover peaceful enjoyment of property and protection from discrimination or harassment.

# Understanding your tenancy agreement in Wales
...
This advice applies to Wales. See advice for See advice for England, See advice for Northern Ireland, See advice for Scotland
...
The tenancy agreement is a contract between you and your landlord. It may be written or verbal. The tenancy agreement gives certain rights to both you and your landlord. For example, your right to occupy the accommodation and your landlord’s right to receive rent for letting the accommodation.
...
You and your landlord may have made arrangements about the tenancy, and these will be part of the tenancy agreement as long as they do not conflict with law. Both you and your landlord have rights and responsibilities given by law. The tenancy agreement can give both you and your landlord more than your statutory rights, but can't give you less than your statutory rights. If a term in the tenancy agreement gives either you or your landlord less than your statutory rights, that term cannot be enforced.
...
Most tenants do not have a right in law to a written tenancy agreement. However, social housing landlords such as local authorities and housing associations will normally give you a written tenancy agreement.
...
There are obligations you and your landlord have which may not be set down in the agreement but which are given by law and are implied into all tenancy agreements. These terms form part of the contract, even though they haven't been specifically agreed between your landlord and you.

Your, or your landlord’s, right to end a tenancy agreement and your right to stay and be protected from eviction will depend on the type of tenancy you have.
...
## Is the tenancy agreement ‘unfair’
...
The tenancy agreement is a form of consumer contract and as such it must be in plain language which is clear and easy to understand. It must not contain any terms which could be ‘unfair’.

pages.summary:
Summary:

- Purpose: This Citizens Advice guide explains tenancy agreements in Wales, covering what the contract means for renters and landlords, rights and responsibilities, and how Welsh law applies.
- Key points:
  - A tenancy agreement is a contract (written or verbal) between you and your landlord, outlining rights to occupy and the landlord’s right to receive rent.
  - Terms cannot reduce your statutory rights; you can rely on legal minimums even if the agreement says otherwise.
  - Not all tenants have a written agreement, but social housing (local authorities, housing associations) usually provides one.
  - Implied terms exist in all tenancy agreements, even if not written, and these are legally binding.
  - Landlords must provide a valid address in England or Wales (or a second address in England/Wales if their main is elsewhere).
  - Any rights guaranteed by law override terms in the agreement; the contract cannot negate statutory rights.
- Ending the tenancy: Your ability to end the tenancy and protection from eviction depends on the tenancy type.
- Fairness and clarity: Tenancy agreements must be in plain language and free from unfair terms (as consumer contracts).
- Non-discrimination: Landlords must not discriminate on protected characteristics (disability, gender reassignment, pregnancy/maternity, race, religion/belief, sex, sexual orientation).

If you need, I can tailor this to your specific tenancy type (e.g., assured, assured shorthold, social housing) or extract Wales-specific statutory rights and proofreading tips for a plain-language agreement.

Summary:

- The lease defines how service charges are organized and what can be charged. If you pay a service charge, you have the right to:
  - Request a summary showing how the charge is calculated and what it’s spent on.
  - See supporting documents (e.g., receipts).
  - Have the landlord provide this information; failing to do so is a criminal offence.

- Ground rent: The landlord can only increase ground rent if you agree or the lease allows it.

- Insurance: You have the right to:
  - Request a summary of the insurance policy.
  - Challenge the cost via a tribunal if you think it’s unreasonable.

- Consultation and costs: You have rights to be consulted about charges for running or maintaining the building if you’re asked to pay more than a certain amount. Landlords must follow a formal “Section 20” process. If proper consultation isn’t done, there’s a limit on what you may have to pay—seek advice from the Leasehold Advisory Service.

- Disputing charges:
  - You may apply to a tribunal if you believe a charge is unreasonable, the related work quality is poor, or you should not be paying at all.
  - You cannot apply if you’ve already agreed to pay, if the dispute is already in court, or if you pay a fixed charge.
  - Landlords can take court action if you stop paying a charge you’re responsible for.

- Where to get help: The Leasehold Advisory Service provides guidance; Citizens Advice and GOV.UK also offer official information on leasehold rights and charges. If you’re seeking challenge routes, tribunals, and detailed consultation rules, these sources are the recommended starting points (including England-specific guidance).

Summary:
This GOV.UK guidance explains typical leasehold charges in England, including ground rent and service charges, and how they are set and charged under a lease. Key points:
- Ground rent: a fee payable to the freeholder if the lease requires it, usually annually; the lease specifies the amount and any future increases; a formal demand must give a payment date 30–60 days from issue, and backdated demands for up to 6 years may be possible.
- Service charges: payments to cover costs of services for the building and shared areas (maintenance, repairs, building insurance, cleaning, etc.); the lease should detail what is charged for, when to pay, and, for existing properties, the previous two years’ charges to show cost trends; charges must be reasonably incurred and for work/services of a reasonable standard.
- Demands: both ground rent and service charges are only payable when the lease requires it and a formal demand is issued; charges must be reasonable and supported by records.
- Disputes: challenging a leasehold charge or applying to a Tribunal can be time-consuming and costly with no guaranteed success; seek advice (e.g., Leasehold Advisory Service, Citizens Advice) before pursuing a tribunal.

Context: Official guidance from the CMA in association with the Leasehold Advisory Service, relevant to England.

Summary:

- The page explains leasehold property basics in England, focusing on two ongoing costs: ground rent and service charges.
- Ground rent: a fee you may pay to the landlord if your lease started before 30 June 2022; the amount and due dates are set out in your lease. The Leasehold Reform (Ground Rent) Act 2022 bans administration fees for collecting ground rent that is restricted by the Act, effective 30 June 2022.

- Administration and other charges: landlords may charge for permissions to alter property, document access, late or non-payment charges, or breaches of lease covenants.
- Financial planning: check mortgage eligibility and potential Help to Buy options; budget for ground rent and service charges; consider other costs like ground rent (if applicable) and any admin fees.

If your goal is direct guidance, focus on:
- What your lease requires for ground rent and any caps or changes post-2022.
- What services are charged to you and the corresponding service charge components.
- Any admin fees you might be charged and what the law permits (noting the 2022 Act exclusions).
- Steps to manage payments or seek help if you’re in arrears.

# What is ground rent?

## In this guide

- What is ground rent?
- - Cost of ground rent
- Who pays ground rent
- Ground rent demand notices
- Ground rent increases
- How you can reduce your ground rent
- If you do not pay ground rent that you owe
- Future changes to leasehold law and ground rent

Hide

Ground rent is a payment a leaseholder makes to the freeholder (landlord) as a condition of their lease.

When you own a leasehold property, you own the property for the length of the lease, but you do not own the land it’s built on. You may need to pay ground rent each year for the right to occupy the land.

If you do not pay ground rent that you owe, you could be breaching the terms of your lease.

Ground rent is separate from service charges, which you pay for services the landlord provides to maintain the building.

## Cost of ground rent

Whether you'll need to pay ground rent depends on your lease.

Your lease will set out the amount of any ground rent you pay, when you pay it and how any increases are calculated.

It’s often a fairly small amount, such as £50 or £100 a year.

But some leases allow it to increase to a high amount that could cause problems such as affecting the value of the property.

There are things you can do if high ground rent is a problem for your property.

# Reasons for challenging a service charge

## In this guide

- Reasons for challenging a service charge
- How to challenge your service charge
- Applying to the tribunal

Hide

You can challenge a service charge for a leasehold property if:

- the landlord did not follow the correct process for issuing the demand
- the terms of your lease do not require you to pay the charge (it’s best to get legal advice on this as leases can be complex)
- you think the cost is not reasonable
- you do not think the service or work was done to a reasonable standard
- you do not think the work was necessary
- you think the work could have been done over time to spread high costs
- you think the work was only needed because of the landlord’s negligence, such as a failure to properly maintain the building
- the landlord did not follow the correct process for consulting leaseholders about major works, and you lost money or rights as a result
- the landlord did not issue their demand in time (there is a time limit for recovering service charge costs)

If your challenge progresses to a tribunal or court you will need to prove your grounds for challenging the charge.

There is no set time limit for challenging a service charge, but it's best to raise any concerns within a reasonable time.

Find out what can be included in service charges

You can use your legal rights to ask for information about your service charge to help you decide whether the charge is reasonable.

Summary focused on your query: England challenge service charge increase; housing/leaseholder rights; official guidance sources (Citizens Advice, GOV.UK, Housing Ombudsman)

- Key rights and grounds
  - Service charges must be reasonable under the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985.
  - Costs must be incurred for works/services that meet a reasonable standard; both landlord and leaseholder can apply to a tribunal to decide reasonableness.
  - If costs were incurred more than 18 months ago, you do not have to pay (the 18-month rule). A landlord can issue demands within 18 months, and there are nuances if a notice is served.
  - Costs charged through service charges must still meet the reasonableness test even if they fall under the 18-month rule or notice procedures.

- Tribunal routes and protections
  - Either party can apply to a tribunal to challenge whether a service charge is reasonable.
  - Section 20C applications exist to prevent landlords from adding their legal costs for tribunal proceedings to service charges (and similar protections apply if the landlord seeks a decision on reasonableness).
  - If a landlord seeks to recover costs via service charges, you can request the tribunal also decide not to add the landlord’s legal costs to the service charges.

- Consultation requirements and limits
  - If planned works/services would cost any one leaseholder more than set thresholds (consultation requirements apply). If the landlord fails to consult, limits (e.g., £250 or £100) may apply to individual leaseholders unless tribunal permission is granted. Tribunal permission is typically unlikely if non-consultation did not cause you loss of money or rights.
  - Even where consultation applies, charges remain service charges and must comply with reasonableness standards.

- Practical steps for homeowners/leaseholders
  - Review your lease and the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 requirements for reasonableness, consultation, and timing (18-month rule).
  - If you believe a service charge is unreasonable, file a tribunal challenge (you or your landlord can initiate); cite Section 20C if you want to prevent recovery of the landlord’s legal costs in tribunal proceedings.
  - If a dispute is about recent charges, check whether 18-month limits or consultation requirements were met; if not, your exposure to charges may be limited or challenged.

- Official guidance sources to consult
  - GOV.UK / Citizens Advice: Guidance on service charges and reasonable costs, tribunal routes, and the 18-month rule.
  - Lease Advice (as a resource summarizing rules and processes) for practical steps and examples.
  - Housing Ombudsman: Handles complaints about landlords and property management; useful for broader landlord-tenant issues but not a substitute for legal action at tribunal.

If you want, I can tailor this to your exact scenario (e.g., a specific charge you’re facing, whether consultation occurred, or if you’re near the 18-month window) and point you to the precise GOV.UK and Citizens Advice pages.

# Complain to the Energy Ombudsman

This advice applies to England. See advice for See advice for Northern Ireland, See advice for Scotland, See advice for Wales

## Help us improve our website

Take 5 minutes to tell us if you found what you needed on our website. Your feedback will help us give millions of people the information they need.

You can complain to the Energy Ombudsman if you’ve already complained to your energy company and either:

you’re not happy with their decision

you’ve not been given a decision within 8 weeks

The Energy Ombudsman is independent and can:

get the supplier to look at your complaint again

decide that the supplier made the right decision

force the supplier to give you a response to your complaint

In some instances, they might tell your supplier to give you financial compensation.

## When you can complain

You must complain to the Energy Ombudsman within 12 months of your supplier telling you their decision. If your supplier hasn't given you a decision you might have longer than 12 months, but it's still worth complaining as soon as you can.

## How to complain

You can register your complaint to the Energy Ombudsman:

on their website

on the phone

in a letter you post to them

Find out more about registering your complaint with the Energy Ombudsman on their website.

If you need to communicate in a different way, for example using braille or a different language, you can check accessibility options on the Energy Ombudsman website.

## Further help

The Citizens Advice consumer service can give you advice about:

making a complaint to the Energy Ombudsman

taking the complaint further if you disagree with the Energy Ombudsman’s decision

If you accept the Energy Ombudsman's decision, they'll close the complaint and you won't be able to change the decision.

Check how to contact the Citizens Advice consumer service.

You can also contact the Energy Ombudsman if you need more information. Find contact details on the Energy Ombudsman website.

## Help us improve our website

Take 5 minutes to tell us if you found what you needed on our website. Your feedback will help us give millions of people the information they need.

pages.summary:
If you’re in England and need to dispute a mobile, phone, internet or TV bill, Citizens Advice outlines practical steps and rights:

- Check if you’ve been charged too much or if fraud affects your bill. Contact your provider to request a reduction.
- Billing limit: If your contract started, was renewed, or extended after 1 Oct 2018, you can set a billing limit. If charged above this limit without consent, you don’t have to pay the excess and can ask for the bill to be reduced to the limit.
- How to dispute: Contact the provider with details of why you think the bill is wrong. Use the contact options on the provider’s site (phone, address, email, or webchat).
- If unsatisfied with the provider’s response: Use their internal complaints procedure. If you still disagree, you can escalate to an Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) scheme. Check which ADR scheme your provider uses on the Ofcom website.
- Late payment charges: If your dispute is ongoing or unresolved, you may still incur late payment charges per the provider’s terms.
- If you need extra help: Citizens Advice consumer helpline: 0808 223 1133, or use their online form.

This guidance is for England, with separate guidance available for Northern Ireland, Scotland, and Wales.

The page explains how UK consumers can complain about phone or broadband services and when to use alternative dispute resolution (ADR). Key points:
- Start with your provider’s customer services, then submit a formal complaint (details typically on your bill, provider website, or via customer services).
- If unresolved after six weeks or you receive a deadlock letter (within 12 months), you can use an ADR scheme for free. ADRs are independent and impartial.
- Providers must have an accessible complaints code of practice outlining how they handle complaints, contact methods, investigation steps, and timeframes, plus information on escalating to an ADR if needed.
- Ofcom approves two ADR schemes:
  - CISAS (Communication & Internet Services Adjudication Scheme) for providers like NOW, O2, Sky, SMARTY, TalkTalk, Three, Virgin Media, Vodafone, VOXI.
  - Communications Ombudsman (formerly Ombudsman Services) for providers like BT, EE, GiffGaff, iD Mobile, Lebara, Plusnet, Tesco Mobile, Utility Warehouse, Lyca Mobile.
- If your provider isn’t listed, check with the ADR schemes to determine their scheme.

pages.summary:
Summary:
The page explains Ofcom’s guidance for complaints about changing or switching broadband providers in the UK. Key points:

- Problems when switching: If you encounter issues when switching to a new broadband provider, follow the step-by-step process outlined by Ofcom.
- Steps to resolve with your provider:
  1) Contact your provider’s customer services to explain the problem.
  2) If unresolved, file a formal complaint with the provider (details are on your bill, their website, or by asking customer services).
  3) If still unresolved, request a deadlock letter to escalate to an Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) scheme.
- ADR schemes: There are two schemes— CISAS and the Communications Ombudsman. All providers must belong to one. Your provider will tell you which scheme it uses; you can also check via Ofcom’s ADR checker. If six weeks have passed since your formal complaint, you can contact the ADR directly.
- Escalation to Ofcom: If problems remain, you can complain to Ofcom. While Ofcom does not investigate individual cases, complaints can trigger investigations or enforcement actions.
- Number porting: Providers must allow you to port (keep) your telephone number when switching. If porting is delayed or blocked, contact your new provider. You may be given an Ofcom complaint reference to start a short investigation.
- Extra support: An independent industry panel can review cases and may override the old provider to complete porting if needed.

Helpful for: UK residents (England) seeking official guidance on complaints about broadband provider changes, including steps, ADR options, and how to escalate to Ofcom. For Citizens Advice or GOV.UK context, this Ofcom guidance can be used as the official pathway if you’re experiencing switching problems.
